pronunciation-spelling.title_tr: Pronunciation and Spelling (ij, ui, and the G sound)
pronunciation-spelling.intro_tr: Dutch spelling is largely phonetic once you learn its sound-letter conventions, but a few combinations trip up English speakers immediately: the diphthongs ij and ui, and the guttural g/ch sound that does not exist in English at all. ij and ei are pronounced identically in standard Dutch (roughly like the 'ey' in "they" but shorter), so many word pairs are true homophones and must simply be memorized by spelling. ui is a uniquely Dutch rounded diphthong with no English equivalent; think of starting an "ow" sound but rounding your lips like for "oo". The g (and its written twin ch) is a raspy fricative made at the back of the throat, pronounced harder in the North of the Netherlands and softer/more palatal in the South (Belgium, Limburg). This page also covers the closely related short/long vowel doubling rule (a/aa, e/ee, o/oo, u/uu), since it explains why some vowels double in spelling while ij, ui, ei, eu, oe, ie never do.

de-het-articles.intro_tr: Every Dutch noun belongs to one of two grammatical genders, and this gender decides which definite article it takes: common-gender nouns (the historical merger of masculine and feminine) use 'de', while neuter nouns use 'het'. Roughly two-thirds of all Dutch nouns are de-words, so 'de' is the statistically safer guess when you don't know a noun's gender. Crucially, ALL plural nouns take 'de', no matter what article they had in the singular. The indefinite article 'een' (a/an) is identical for both genders, so gender only becomes visible with definite articles, adjective endings, and pronoun replacement. There is no single foolproof rule, but semantic categories and word endings give strong, memorizable clues, and gender must ultimately be learned per noun (dictionaries mark het-words with 'het' or 'o.' for 'onzijdig').

plural-forms.intro_tr: Dutch nouns form their plural in one of two main ways: adding **-en** (the default and most common ending) or adding **-s** (used mainly after certain unstressed final syllables and after vowels). Adding -en often triggers spelling changes to keep vowels long or short exactly as they were pronounced in the singular; this is the same open/closed syllable spelling logic used throughout Dutch. A smaller, closed set of nouns takes the irregular ending **-eren**, and a handful of very common nouns change their stem vowel entirely (schip → schepen). There is no official phonetic transcription system for Dutch, so pronunciation notes below are described in words rather than in a phonetic reading.

personal-pronouns.intro_tr: Dutch personal pronouns come in three main sets; subject, object, and possessive; and, unusually for English speakers, most of them have two forms: a full/stressed form (used for emphasis, contrast, or standing alone) and a reduced/unstressed form (the everyday spoken default, often written with an apostrophe when contracted). There is also a formal pronoun, u, used for polite address regardless of number, and a written-norm distinction between hen and hun for "them" that many native speakers blur in casual speech. Possessive pronouns function as adjectives before nouns (mijn boek) but also have separate standalone forms (het mijne) for "mine." Reflexive pronouns (me, je, zich, ons) are needed for reflexive verbs like zich wassen. Mastering which form to use; and when to reduce it; is essential groundwork for nearly every other Dutch sentence you will build.

present-tense.intro_tr: The Dutch present tense (tegenwoordige tijd) is formed from the verb stem plus person-specific endings, and it does double duty for both the English simple present ("I work") and the English present continuous ("I am working"); Dutch has no separate progressive present tense. Most verbs are perfectly regular: find the stem, then add nothing, -t, or -en depending on the subject. A handful of very high-frequency verbs (zijn, hebben, and the modal verbs) are irregular and must be memorized as full paradigms. Two spelling mechanics govern almost every mistake beginners make: the vowel/consonant adjustment used to build the stem from the infinitive, and the rule that drops the -t from the jij/je form whenever jij/je is inverted after the verb. The present tense is also regularly used to talk about the near future and, in narrative style, to make past events feel vivid (the "historical present").

zijn-hebben.intro_tr: Zijn ("to be") and hebben ("to have") are the two most important irregular verbs in Dutch: you need them constantly on their own, and even more importantly as auxiliary (helper) verbs to build the perfect tense (perfectum) and pluperfect (plusquamperfectum). Both verbs are highly irregular in the present tense, so their forms simply have to be memorized rather than derived from a stem+ending rule. A key beginner trap is knowing which verbs pair with zijn versus hebben when forming the perfect tense; the choice is not random and follows a fairly reliable pattern based on motion or change of state. This page gives you the full conjugation tables, the auxiliary-choice rules, and the many fixed hebben-expressions (honger hebben, gelijk hebben, etc.) where Dutch uses "to have" where English uses "to be".

u can take either heeft or hebt; heeft is slightly more common and formal.

footnotes_tr: Unlike the present tense, jij/je and u never trigger a change here; was and had stay the same whether the pronoun comes before or after the verb.
These past forms are extremely common because zijn and hebben are among the very few Dutch verbs regularly used in the simple past in everyday speech (most other verbs prefer the perfectum).

tables.caption_tr: Choosing the auxiliary for the perfect tense: hebben vs zijn
rows: Most verbs: transitive verbs (with a direct object) and intransitive verbs that do NOT show motion/change of state
Ik heb een boek gelezen. (I have read a book.)
Verbs describing an ongoing activity without a clear endpoint (lopen, zwemmen, fietsen used without a destination; slapen, werken, wonen)
Ik heb gisteren gezwommen. (I swam yesterday.)
Verbs of motion WITH a change of location/destination (gaan, komen, vertrekken, aankomen, reizen naar...)
Ik ben naar Parijs gereisd. (I traveled to Paris.)
Verbs of change of state (worden, groeien, sterven, gebeuren, veranderen)
Hij is oud geworden. (He has grown old.)
A small set of fixed exceptions (blijven, zijn itself, beginnen for some speakers)
Ik ben thuis gebleven. (I stayed home.)
zijn and hebben as main verbs also use zijn as their own auxiliary
Ik ben moe geweest. (I have been tired.) / Ik heb geluk gehad. (I have had luck.)
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: if the verb shows movement FROM one place/state TO another (a clear destination or result), use zijn; otherwise use hebben.

Note the irony: hebben itself takes hebben as its auxiliary (ik heb gehad), while zijn takes zijn as its own auxiliary (ik ben geweest); this is one of the very few verbs whose past participle (geweest) does not resemble its infinitive at all.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed expressions: hebben + noun (where English often uses 'to be' + adjective)
footnotes_tr: This is a major beginner trap: English speakers instinctively reach for zijn ('I am hungry' → ik ben honger, WRONG). The correct pattern is always hebben + noun: ik heb honger.

word-order-v2.intro_tr: Dutch main clauses follow the strict "V2" (verb-second) rule: no matter what element opens the sentence; subject, time phrase, object, adverb, or even an entire subordinate clause; the finite (conjugated) verb must occupy exactly the second position of the clause. If anything other than the subject fills position 1, the subject is pushed to position 3, right after the verb (this is called inversion). Only ONE constituent, however long, may occupy position 1; it can be a single word or a whole phrase/clause. Any other verbs in the sentence (infinitives, past participles, separable prefixes) are pushed to the very end of the clause, forming a "verb cluster" that brackets the sentence around position 2. This is fundamentally different from English, which keeps SVO order almost regardless of what comes first; a major source of beginner mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: The Core V2 Pattern: The Finite Verb Never Moves Out of Position 2

negation-niet-geen.intro_tr: Dutch has two basic negation words, and choosing the right one depends entirely on what you are negating, not on meaning. Use "geen" to negate a noun that would otherwise be introduced by "een" (a/an) or by no article at all (plurals, mass nouns). Use "niet" for everything else: definite nouns (de/het), verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositional phrases, and past participles/infinitives at the end of a clause. A frequent beginner trap is negating the object of a fixed preposition (like "houden van", "wachten op") with "niet" even though the noun itself has no article. Word order for "niet" is flexible and follows a few predictable placement rules, while "geen" simply replaces the article and stays glued to its noun.

question-formation.intro_tr: Dutch forms questions mainly through word order rather than special auxiliary verbs; there is no equivalent of English "do you...?". Yes/no questions are made by simply inverting the verb and subject (Woon je hier? = "Live you here?"), while wh-questions place the question word first, followed immediately by the verb, then the subject. Separable verb prefixes and other sentence parts still go to the end of the question, just as in statements. Embedded (indirect) questions, however, follow subordinate-clause word order with the verb pushed to the very end. Tag questions and softening particles are also common in spoken Dutch to make questions more polite or conversational.

numbers-time.intro_tr: Dutch numbers and time expressions have several patterns that differ noticeably from English. Cardinal numbers from 21 onward are built by placing the unit before the ten (eenentwintig = "one-and-twenty" = 21), and numbers ending in a vowel like twee/drie require a trema (ë) when combined. Ordinal numbers mostly add -de, but a handful of irregular forms and the -ste ending for 20+ need to be memorized. The biggest trap for English speakers is telling time: "half vier" means 3:30 (half towards four), not 4:30, and minutes between the quarter-hour and half-hour are counted relative to "half" rather than the full hour. This page gives full reference tables for cardinals, ordinals, large numbers, and every 5-minute time expression in a full hour cycle.

adjective-inflection.intro_tr: In Dutch, an adjective placed directly in front of a noun (the "attributive" position) usually adds the ending -e, but there is one key exception: with singular het-words used indefinitely (typically after een, geen, or no article at all), the adjective stays in its bare, uninflected form. De-words always take -e in the singular, and every plural noun takes -e regardless of gender. When an adjective stands after a verb like zijn, worden, or lijken ("predicative" position), it never takes -e at all. A closed set of adjectives; material words ending in -en (houten, gouden) and certain vowel-final loanwords (oranje, roze, gratis); never inflect, in any position. Adding -e can also trigger small spelling adjustments to the adjective's stem (vowel/consonant doubling, f→v, s→z), which are listed separately below. This page only covers the written -e ending; Dutch has no official phonetic transcription system, so pronunciation notes are kept minimal.

modal-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen, and the negative-only hoeven) express ability, obligation, desire, permission, and future/intention. They are irregular in the present tense singular and are almost always followed by a bare infinitive at the end of the clause, without 'te'. In compound tenses (perfect, pluperfect) modals combine with another infinitive rather than a past participle, producing the characteristic "double infinitive" (IPP) construction. Getting the difference between 'moeten niet' (should not) and 'hoeven niet/geen' (don't need to) right is one of the most common trouble spots for learners. This page gives full conjugation tables, meanings, past-tense forms, word order patterns, and typical mistakes.

separable-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch separable verbs (scheidbare werkwoorden) are verbs formed from a prefix + a base verb, where the prefix carries the main stress (OPbellen, AANkomen) and can detach from the verb and move to the end of the clause. In a main clause with a finite verb form, the prefix splits off and jumps to the very end; in a subordinate clause the whole verb stays glued together at the clause-final position. In the perfect tense, "ge-" is inserted between the prefix and the participle (opgebeld, not geopbeld), and with "te" + infinitive, "te" is inserted the same way (op te bellen). Recognizing which prefixes are separable versus inseparable, and mastering the word-order rules, is essential because getting this wrong is one of the most common mistakes for learners.

perfect-tense.intro_tr: The perfectum (present perfect) is the tense Dutch speakers use most often in conversation to talk about completed past events; far more common in speech than the imperfectum (simple past). It is built with a conjugated form of hebben or zijn plus a past participle (voltooid deelwoord), and the participle is always pushed to the very end of the clause. Choosing the right auxiliary is a key skill: most verbs take hebben, but verbs expressing motion toward a destination or a change of state typically take zijn. Regular participles are formed with ge- + stem + t/d according to the so-called 't kofschip' rule, while a large set of very frequent verbs have irregular participles that simply have to be memorized. Word order rules (participle at the end, auxiliary and participle clustering together in subordinate clauses) are just as important as choosing the correct form.

imperfect-tense.intro_tr: The imperfectum (simple past / imperfect tense) is the second past tense in Dutch, used mainly in continuous speech and writing to narrate sequences of past events, describe repeated or habitual past actions, and set the background of a story (similar to English "walked", "was", "used to do"). It is formed differently for weak verbs (regular, add -te(n)/-de(n) to the stem) and strong verbs (irregular, change the stem vowel), plus a small set of fully irregular verbs like zijn and hebben that must be memorized. Unlike the perfectum, the imperfectum does not use an auxiliary verb; it is a single conjugated form. Whether to add -te(n) or -de(n) to a weak verb depends on the final consonant of the stem, remembered with the mnemonic 't kofschip. In everyday spoken Dutch the perfectum is often preferred for single completed events, but the imperfectum is essential for storytelling, written narrative, and modal verbs.

subordinate-clauses.title_tr: Subordinate Clauses and Verb-Final Word Order
subordinate-clauses.intro_tr: A subordinate clause (bijzin) cannot stand alone; it depends on a main clause and is introduced by a subordinating conjunction such as dat, omdat, als, or terwijl. The rule that most often trips up English speakers is verb-final word order: inside a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb; and any other verbs stacked with it; move all the way to the end of the clause, instead of staying in second position as in a main clause. When a sentence opens with the subordinate clause, the main clause that follows it shows inversion (verb comes before the subject). Separable verbs never split in a subordinate clause; they stay joined together as one word at the very end. When two or more verbs pile up at the end (modal + infinitive, or auxiliary + past participle), their internal order follows its own pattern.

er-usage.intro_tr: The little word "er" is one of the most distinctive features of Dutch grammar, and it has no single English equivalent; depending on context it can mean "there", "it/them", or nothing translatable at all. At the beginner (A2) level, you need to recognize its five core functions: (1) existential subject ("there is/are"), (2) unstressed locative "there" referring back to a place, (3) a pronominal element fused with a preposition (e.g. eraan, erover) when referring to things rather than people, (4) partitive "er" required after numbers or quantity words that refer to something already mentioned, and (5) the dummy subject of an impersonal passive sentence. Unlike in English, Dutch "er" in functions 1, 4, and 5 is grammatically obligatory and cannot simply be omitted. This page gives you an overview of all five uses with clear patterns and common mistakes; deeper rules for combining multiple "er"-functions in one clause, and the fuller pronominal-adverb system, are covered in separate advanced topics.

comparatives.intro_tr: Dutch adjectives change form to express comparison, just like English "small – smaller – smallest." The comparative is formed by adding -er and the superlative by adding -st, but a handful of spelling adjustments (consonant doubling, the -der rule for adjectives ending in -r) and several irregular forms have to be learned separately. Unequal comparisons use dan ("than"), while equal comparisons use even/net zo … als ("as … as"). Superlatives take de or het before the noun depending on gender/number when used attributively, but predicative and adverbial superlatives (after zijn or a verb) almost always use het, regardless of the noun's own gender. This page gives you the full formation rules, the irregular forms, the spelling exceptions, and the standard comparison sentence patterns.

future-tense.intro_tr: Dutch has no single dedicated future tense form; instead speakers combine an auxiliary verb with an infinitive, or simply use the present tense. **gaan + infinitive** is the everyday choice for plans, intentions, and predictions based on present evidence ("it's going to..."). **zullen + infinitive** is used for promises, spontaneous decisions, offers, formal predictions, and (with the word "wel") for guesses about the present rather than the future. Very often, especially with a time expression like "morgen" or "volgende week", Dutch simply uses the **present tense**, which sounds more natural than either construction for scheduled events. As with all modal-style constructions, the infinitive is pushed to the very end of the clause.

diminutives.intro_tr: Dutch diminutives are formed by adding a suffix (based on -je) to a noun, most commonly to indicate small size, but very often instead to express affection, informality, or to soften a request. The exact suffix (-je, -tje, -pje, -etje, or -kje) depends entirely on the sound the base noun ends in, and there are several irregular forms that must simply be memorized. Every diminutive noun, no matter what its original gender was, becomes a het-word, and its plural is always formed with -s. Diminutives are extremely frequent in everyday spoken Dutch, so recognizing and forming them correctly is essential even at a beginner level.

reflexive-verbs.intro_tr: Dutch reflexive verbs (wederkerende werkwoorden) are verbs used with a reflexive pronoun that refers back to the subject, roughly matching English "myself, yourself, himself..." but Dutch uses the reflexive pronoun far more often than English does, even where English has no reflexive word at all (e.g. "zich vergissen" = "to be mistaken", not "to mistake oneself"). Some verbs are truly reflexive and never appear without their reflexive pronoun, while others are optionally reflexive and change meaning or add a "self-directed" nuance when the pronoun is added. The reflexive pronoun has an unstressed everyday form (me, je, zich, ons) and an emphatic form with -zelf, and its position in the sentence follows the normal rules for object pronouns (right after the conjugated verb or subject, before a separable particle, always with "hebben" in the perfect tense). This page gives the full pronoun paradigm, verb lists, meaning-changing pairs, word-order patterns, and the key contrast between reflexive "zich" and reciprocal "elkaar".

passive-voice.intro_tr: The Dutch passive voice (lijdende vorm) is formed with the auxiliary verb worden plus a past participle, and it shifts the focus from who performs an action to who or what receives it (e.g., 'De brief wordt geschreven' = 'The letter is being written'). Worden-passive expresses a dynamic action in progress or occurring, which is different from the zijn-passive that describes a resulting state (covered separately). Every tense of the passive is built by conjugating worden itself into that tense, then attaching the past participle at the end of the clause. The agent (the 'doer') is optionally introduced with door ('by'), never with bij. In perfect and pluperfect passive tenses, worden's own past participle 'geworden' is grammatically correct but almost always dropped in practice, which is why 'De brief is geschreven' can mean both 'the letter has been written' (action) and 'the letter is written/finished' (state) depending on context.

conditional.intro_tr: Dutch conditional sentences are built with the conjunction "als" ("if") introducing a condition clause, often paired with "zou" ("would") in the result clause for hypothetical situations. There are three main types: Type 0 (general truths, present + present), Type 1 (real future possibilities, present + present/future), and Type 2 (hypothetical present/future, past tense + zou + infinitive). Word order is crucial: the verb goes to the end of the als-clause (subordinate order), and if the als-clause comes first, the main clause that follows must have inversion (verb before subject), often signalled by the word "dan". "Als" can even be dropped entirely, with the verb moving to the front of the condition clause instead; a common pattern especially in speech and instructions. "Zou/zouden" is technically the imperfectum (past tense) of "zullen" and is the standard way to express "would" in Dutch.

relative-clauses.intro_tr: Dutch relative clauses (bijzinnen met betrekkelijk voornaamwoord) attach extra information to a noun using the pronouns die, dat, or waar. The choice between die and dat depends entirely on the grammatical gender of the antecedent noun (de-word vs. het-word) and whether it is singular or plural; it has nothing to do with people vs. things, unlike English "who" vs. "which". Waar is used instead of a preposition + which/where, especially for places and things, while people after a preposition use "preposition + wie" instead. As in all Dutch subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb is pushed to the very end of the relative clause. This topic is essential at B1 level because relative clauses appear constantly in written and spoken Dutch to combine and elaborate sentences.

aan-het-progressive.title_tr: Progressive Aspect: aan het + Infinitive, zitten/staan te
aan-het-progressive.intro_tr: Dutch has no single grammatical continuous tense like English "-ing", but it expresses ongoing, in-progress action with periphrastic (multi-word) constructions built on the verb "zijn" (to be). The most common and stylistically neutral pattern is "zijn + aan het + infinitive" (e.g. "Ik ben aan het eten" = "I am eating"), which can be used in present or past time by changing the form of "zijn". A more vivid, descriptive alternative uses a posture verb; "zitten", "staan", "liggen", or "lopen"; followed by "te + infinitive"; this construction adds information about the physical position or manner of the subject (sitting, standing, lying, walking around) and is common in spoken, informal Dutch. Both constructions emphasize that an action is happening at a specific moment, in contrast to the simple present tense, which is used for habitual or general statements. Word order changes in subordinate clauses, where the finite verb ("zijn", "zit", "staat", etc.) moves to the very end of the clause.

om-te-infinitive.intro_tr: The "om ... te + infinitive" structure is the Dutch equivalent of English "in order to" or simply "to" before a verb, and it is one of the most frequent patterns for expressing purpose, necessity, or evaluation. "Om" opens the clause, any objects or adverbials come in the middle, and "te + infinitive" always closes the clause, with the infinitive in final position. "Om" is grammatically required whenever the infinitive clause contains extra material (an object, adverbial, or complement) or follows an adjective/noun construction like "het is moeilijk om..." or "de kans om...", but it is dropped after a small set of verbs (proberen, beginnen, hopen, weigeren, durven, beloven, vergeten) that take a bare "te + infinitive". With separable verbs, "te" is inserted between the detachable prefix and the verb stem (e.g., "om op te bellen"). Getting the placement of "om", "te", negation words, and separable prefixes right is a key B1 milestone, since mixing this up with the bare infinitive used after modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen) is one of the most common learner errors.

Ik heb geen tijd om te helpen.

Hij is te jong om te stemmen.
He is too young to vote.
Ze is oud genoeg om te rijden.
She is old enough to drive.
Je hebt de kans om te winnen.

Wij hopen te winnen. (We hope to win.)
Hij besluit te vertrekken. (He decides to leave.)
Ze weigert te betalen. (She refuses to pay.)
Ik beloof te helpen. (I promise to help.)
Hij durft niet te springen. (He doesn't dare to jump.)

rows: modal verbs: kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen, gaan, laten, zien, horen
proberen, beginnen, hopen, weigeren, durven, beloven, vergeten, staan/zitten/liggen te
purpose clauses, adjective + om, noun + om

Hij vertrekt vroeg om op tijd aan te komen.

Hij haast zich om zich niet te verlaten.

examples.target: Hij is te moe om te koken.

examples.note_tr: Fixed pattern: te + adjective + om + te + infinitive.

examples.target: Ik probeer elke dag te sporten.

examples.note_tr: After 'proberen' no 'om' is used; just 'te + infinitive'.

examples.target: We bellen om je uit te nodigen voor het feest.

examples.note_tr: Classic purpose construction: main clause + om + object + te + infinitive.

imperative-mood.intro_tr: The Dutch imperative (gebiedende wijs) is used to give commands, instructions, requests, and advice. Unlike English, Dutch normally forms the imperative from the bare present-tense stem (the same form used with 'ik') and drops the subject pronoun entirely; there is no separate singular/plural or person distinction. A handful of common verbs (zijn, hebben) have irregular imperative stems that don't match their normal 'ik' form. Negation uses niet or geen just like in statements, and separable verbs split apart with the prefix moving to the end of the clause. In everyday speech, Dutch speakers soften bare commands with small particles like eens, even, maar, and toch, which make an order sound like a friendly request rather than a blunt demand; this is a key feature of natural spoken Dutch that has no direct English equivalent.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the imperative (regular verbs)
footnotes_tr: The imperative stem is formed exactly like the 'ik' form of the present tense: drop -en from the infinitive and apply the usual spelling rules (open/closed syllable, v→f, z→s).
No -t, -en, or any other ending is added; the bare stem is the command form for everyone, one person or many.

tables.caption_tr: Irregular and special imperatives
rows: Completely irregular; 'zij' is never used as a command.
Rare alone; usually combined, e.g. 'Heb geduld!' (Have patience!)
Regular, very frequent in commands ('Ga weg!')
Regular, common in separable verbs ('Sta op!')
Regular, extremely common ('Doe het licht aan!')
Rarely used as a plain command (e.g. formal 'Word lid!' = Become a member!)

footnotes_tr: Adding -t before 'u' (Komt u binnen) is the most traditionally 'correct' polite form, but many speakers simply use the bare stem with 'u' added after it (Kom binnen, mevrouw) in everyday polite speech.

tables.caption_tr: Negative imperative: niet vs. geen
rows: Don't take a risk / any risk!

tables.caption_tr: Imperative with separable verbs
rows: Put on your coat! / Don't put on your coat!
footnotes_tr: Just like in the present tense, the separable prefix detaches and moves to the very end of the imperative clause.

tables.caption_tr: Softening particles commonly added to commands
rows: makes it sound like a casual, one-time request
'just for a moment', friendly and low-effort
footnotes_tr: Particles can be combined, e.g. 'Kom nou toch eens hier!'; very natural in spoken Dutch but this stacking is rare in writing.
None of these particles change the verb form; they are added after the stem (and after any object) to adjust tone only.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with the Dutch imperative
rows: Do not use a subject pronoun with the imperative; the bare stem alone is the command.
zijn has the irregular imperative 'wees', never a form of 'zij'.
Only one 'niet' is needed; place it before the separated prefix, not after.

There is no plural imperative ending; if you want to explicitly address a group with a verb form, use the plain present tense 'Komen jullie binnen?' as a question instead, or just the bare stem 'Kom binnen' for everyone.
Doe dat niet! / Doe dat geen keer!
'geen' negates nouns, not verbs; use 'niet' to negate the action itself.

examples.translation_tr: Come here!
examples.note_tr: Bare stem (kom-), no subject pronoun needed; the most common command form.

examples.target: Wees stil, alsjeblieft.
examples.translation_tr: Be quiet, please.
examples.note_tr: zijn has the irregular imperative 'wees', not 'zij'.

examples.target: Doe het raam even dicht.
examples.translation_tr: Close the window for a second, would you.
examples.note_tr: Separable verb dichtdoen: the prefix 'dicht' moves to the end; 'even' softens the request.

examples.target: Loop niet zo hard!
examples.translation_tr: Don't walk so fast!
examples.note_tr: Negative imperative with niet placed right before the element being negated.

examples.target: Neemt u plaats, meneer.
examples.translation_tr: Please have a seat, sir.
examples.note_tr: Formal imperative: stem + -t, with explicit 'u' after the verb; polite register.

examples.target: Ga niet weg zonder het te zeggen!
examples.translation_tr: Don't leave without saying it!
examples.note_tr: Separable verb weggaan negated: 'weg' stays attached to the end, niet comes before it.

examples.translation_tr: Give me that book, would you.
examples.note_tr: 'eens' softens the command, making it sound like a casual request rather than an order.

examples.target: Kinderen, ruim je speelgoed op!
examples.translation_tr: Children, pick up your toys!
examples.note_tr: The imperative has no plural marking; the same bare stem addresses one person or many.

fixed-prepositions.intro_tr: Many Dutch verbs are always paired with one specific preposition, forming a fixed unit that must be learned together (e.g. wachten op = 'to wait for', denken aan = 'to think of'). The preposition is dictated by the verb, not by logic, so it frequently does not match the English equivalent; English speakers must simply memorize each pair as a chunk. These combinations matter for word order (the preposition stays attached to its verb, even in questions and subordinate clauses), for forming questions (waar+preposition for things, preposition+wie for people), and for referring back to something already mentioned using er/daar+preposition. This topic is the foundation for the more advanced 'pronominal adverbs' (eraan, erop, ermee) and 'preposition nuance' topics later in the curriculum.

rows: I am waiting for the bus.
to pay attention to / watch out for

She is preparing for the exam.
Hij reageerde niet op mijn bericht.
He did not react to my message.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed-preposition verbs with AAN
rows: Je went snel aan het klimaat.
You get used to the climate quickly.
Ze werkt aan een nieuw project.
She is working on a new project.
Hij lijdt aan een zeldzame ziekte.
He suffers from a rare disease.
We beginnen morgen aan de verbouwing.
Ze doet mee aan de wedstrijd.
She takes part in the competition.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed-preposition verbs with VAN, VOOR, and NAAR

Companies benefit from the new law.
Kinderen zijn afhankelijk van hun ouders.
She takes care of her grandmother.
We kiezen voor de goedkoopste optie.
He is searching for his keys.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed-preposition verbs with MET, IN, OVER, TEGEN, and OM

Ze gelooft in een goede afloop.

Hij is geslaagd in zijn opzet.

Denk goed na over je antwoord.

footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: use waar+preposition ONLY for things/ideas; for people you must use preposition+wie. This same split reappears later with pronominal adverbs (er/daar vs. hem/haar/hen).

Daar wacht ik al lang op!

examples.translation_tr: What are you thinking about?

examples.target: Waarop wacht je nog?
examples.translation_tr: What are you still waiting for?

examples.translation_tr: Who are you waiting for?

conjunctions.title_tr: Conjunctions: Main and Subordinate Clause Word Order (want vs omdat)
conjunctions.intro_tr: Dutch conjunctions split into two grammatical families that behave very differently: coordinating conjunctions (like en, maar, want, dus) link two independent clauses and leave normal word order untouched, while subordinating conjunctions (like omdat, als, terwijl) introduce a dependent clause and force the finite verb to jump to the very end of that clause. The classic beginner trap is want vs omdat: both can translate as "because", but want keeps the verb in second position (main-clause order) while omdat sends it to the end (verb-final order). If a subordinate clause is placed first in the sentence, the following main clause must invert its subject and verb. Getting this distinction right is one of the most important building blocks of correct Dutch sentence structure.

Wil je koffie, of wil je thee?
Ik ga slapen, want ik ben moe.
Het regent, dus ik neem een paraplu.
none (often triggers inversion in formal style)
Hij eet noch vlees, noch vis.

No; a want-clause can never start the sentence
Yes; an omdat-clause can start the sentence (triggers inversion in the main clause)
Slightly more conversational, presents an independent justification
Neutral/standard, presents the reason as logically dependent
Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben ziek.
Ik blijf thuis, omdat ik ziek ben. / Omdat ik ziek ben, blijf ik thuis.

tables.caption_tr: Word order slot diagram
rows: Main clause after fronted subordinate clause

tables.caption_tr: Frequent beginner mistakes

Verb 'ben' stays in 2nd position as if omdat were coordinating
Ik blijf thuis, omdat ik ziek ben.
Omdat ik ziek ben, ik blijf thuis.

Want ik ben ziek, blijf ik thuis.

examples.translation_tr: I'm staying home, for I am sick.
examples.note_tr: want is coordinating: word order in both clauses stays normal (subject-verb).

examples.target: Ik blijf thuis, omdat ik ziek ben.
examples.translation_tr: I'm staying home because I am sick.
examples.note_tr: omdat is subordinating: the finite verb 'ben' is pushed to the very end of its clause.

examples.translation_tr: Because I am sick, I'm staying home.
examples.note_tr: When the omdat-clause starts the sentence, the main clause inverts: verb 'blijf' comes immediately after the comma, then subject 'ik'.

pronominal-adverbs.intro_tr: Dutch cannot combine a preposition directly with the neutral pronoun "het" to mean "with it" or "about it"; you cannot say "met het" or "aan het" in that sense. Instead, Dutch fuses a special adverb (er, daar, hier, or waar) together with the preposition to form a single word: ermee, eraan, erop, daarmee, waaraan, and so on. These pronominal adverbs replace "preposition + it/that/this/what" whenever the reference is to a thing, idea, or situation; never to a person. The choice of er/daar/hier/waar depends on whether the reference is unstressed and neutral (er), pointed out or contrasted (daar), close by (hier), or part of a question/relative clause (waar). In everyday speech these forms are frequently split apart, with the "er/daar/hier/waar" part moving early in the sentence and the preposition staying near the verb.

footnotes_tr: Note the irregular shape changes: met → mee, tot → toe. All other prepositions simply attach unchanged.
'waarom' as a fused form usually means 'why', not literally 'around what'; check meaning in context.

tables.caption_tr: Which base form to use: er / daar / hier / waar
rows: Default, unstressed, neutral reference to something already known/implied
Stressed, pointing at or contrasting a specific thing already mentioned
Daarmee ben ik het niet eens.
Refers to something close by, present, or just said/shown
With this, the matter is settled.
Used in questions and in relative clauses referring to a thing
footnotes_tr: 'daar-' forms are more emphatic/formal than 'er-' forms and are common in writing and formal speech.
'waar-' forms also start relative clauses: het boek waarover we praatten (the book we were talking about).

rows: I like it. (referring to a thing)
footnotes_tr: This is the single most important rule: never use 'erover hem' or similar; pronominal adverbs are strictly for non-persons.

He's been waiting for it for an hour.
Ik kijk er erg naar uit.
I'm really looking forward to it.
Can stay fused or split: 'Waar praten jullie over?'
With nothing to insert, the form usually stays together.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: Dutch never combines a preposition directly with 'het' meaning 'it' in this sense.
met → mee and tot → toe when fused.
Using pronominal adverb for a person
Pronominal adverbs are only for things/ideas, never for people.
The inserted element (niet, adverbs, time phrases) goes between 'er' and the preposition, not after the whole fused form.

examples.translation_tr: I'm not thinking about it.

examples.target: Waaraan denk je?
examples.translation_tr: What are you thinking about?

examples.target: Daarmee ben ik het niet eens.

examples.target: Ik houd er heel veel van.

indirect-speech.intro_tr: Indirect speech (indirecte rede) reports what someone said or asked without quoting their exact words, using a subordinate clause introduced by dat ("that") for statements or of ("whether/if") for yes/no questions. Because dat and of create a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb (and any auxiliaries) must move to the end of the clause, following Dutch verb-final word order; this is the single biggest structural change from direct speech. When reporting a wh-question (with wie, wat, waar, wanneer, hoe, waarom, etc.), you drop dat/of entirely and use the question word itself as the connector, still keeping the verb at the end. Pronouns, possessives, and time/place expressions often need to shift to match the reporter's perspective, and tense may optionally shift backward ("backshift"), though Dutch is less strict about this than English, especially when the reporting verb is in the present tense.

ik → hij; verb 'is' moves to clause-final position

jij/je → ik (from the perspective of the person being quoted)

possessives-genitive.title_tr: Possessive Structures and the -s Genitive (van, Jans)
possessives-genitive.intro_tr: Dutch marks possession mainly with possessive pronouns (mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons/onze, jullie, hun) placed before the noun, and with the everyday van-construction (de auto van Jan) for common nouns. A genuine -s genitive still exists, but only with proper names (Jans boek, Marie's fiets), and its spelling depends on how the name ends (consonant, vowel, or s/x/z). In casual speech, Dutch also uses a colloquial substitute genitive built with the possessive pronoun after the name (Jan zijn boek, Marie d'r tas), which is widespread but not accepted in formal writing. Older genitive case endings (des, der) survive only in fixed, literary expressions and are covered separately. This page focuses on the pronoun paradigm, the -s genitive rules for names, and the van-construction that replaces the genitive for ordinary nouns.

adverb-formation.title_tr: Degree Adverbs and Intensification (heel, erg, nogal)
adverb-formation.intro_tr: Dutch uses a small set of degree adverbs (bijwoorden van graad); such as heel, erg, and nogal; placed directly in front of an adjective or another adverb to say "very," "quite," or "rather." Unlike English, these words never take an ending and never move away from the word they modify. The tricky part for English speakers is that heel, erg, zeer, nogal, tamelijk, and vrij all roughly translate as "very/quite/rather," but they differ in formality, intensity, and emotional tone; erg in particular carries a slightly negative flavor because it also means "bad" as a plain adjective. This page maps out the full scale from mild ("a little") to extreme ("incredibly"), shows exactly where each word goes in the sentence, and flags the classic pitfalls (heel = "whole" vs. heel = "very"; erg alone = "bad").

pluperfect.intro_tr: The plusquamperfectum (pluperfect, "had gedaan") is the Dutch tense used for an action or state that was already completed before another point in the past; it is the "past of the past". It is formed exactly like the perfectum, but the auxiliary hebben or zijn is put into the imperfectum (had/hadden, was/waren) instead of the present tense (heb/heeft, ben/is). The choice between had and was follows the same rules as for the perfect tense (transitive/stative verbs → hebben; intransitive verbs of movement or change of state → zijn). It is especially common after temporal conjunctions like toen, nadat, and voordat, in reported speech (dat-clauses), and in the "als"-clause of unreal past conditionals. In main clauses the auxiliary occupies the V2 position and the participle goes to the end; in subordinate clauses both the auxiliary and the participle move to the very end of the clause, with the auxiliary last.

conditional-perfect.intro_tr: The conditional perfect (also called the past conditional) describes something that would have happened but did not; an unreal or hypothetical event in the past. It is built by combining the conditional auxiliary zou/zouden with hebben or zijn plus a past participle, essentially the perfect tense shifted into an unreal mood. The choice between hebben and zijn follows the exact same rules as the ordinary perfect tense (perfectum): verbs of motion, change of state, or the verbs zijn/blijven themselves take zijn, while most other verbs take hebben. This form typically appears as the result clause of an unreal past conditional sentence introduced by als, but it is also used independently to express regret, missed chances, or speculation about the past. Note that Dutch allows two accepted word orders for the verb cluster (zou hebben gedaan or zou gedaan hebben), and in everyday speech the als-clause is often simplified to a plain plusquamperfectum (had gedaan).

passive-tenses.intro_tr: Dutch has two distinct passive constructions that both use forms of "worden" and "zijn" alongside a past participle, and English speakers often confuse them because English uses only "to be" for both. The action passive (with worden) describes an event happening TO the subject; wordt/werd (present/imperfect) and is/was (perfect/pluperfect, where "geworden" is silently dropped). The state passive (with zijn) instead describes the resulting condition after the action is finished. Getting "wordt" vs "is" right, and knowing when "geworden" disappears, is the single biggest source of passive-voice errors for learners; this page maps out every tense form so you can check any sentence at a glance.

footnotes_tr: A present-tense state passive ('is gesloten') and a perfect-tense action passive ('is gesloten' from 'wordt gesloten') look IDENTICAL in form; context tells you which meaning is intended.

infinitive-clusters.intro_tr: Dutch uses a special "bare infinitive" construction with the causative verb laten and the perception verbs zien, horen, voelen (and, more loosely, ruiken/zien for smell/sight) to express "to have something done," "to let someone do something," or "to see/hear/feel someone doing something." No "te" is used before the second infinitive; compare this to English "I saw him leave" or "I had my car washed." The single most important rule for this topic is what happens in the perfect tenses: instead of the expected past participle (gelaten, gezien, gehoord, gevoeld), Dutch replaces it with the plain infinitive whenever it is directly followed by another infinitive. This is called the IPP-effect (Infinitivus Pro Participio), also nicknamed the "double infinitive" rule, and it also affects helpen and modal verbs. Word order becomes especially important once you add hebben (perfect tense) or a modal like zou, because then three or more verbs stack up together at the end of the clause.

This same IPP effect also happens with modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen): e.g. 'Ik heb het niet kunnen doen' (I haven't been able to do it), not 'gekund doen'.

laten-causative.intro_tr: The verb "laten" is one of Dutch's most useful and idiomatic verbs: it expresses that the subject causes, allows, or arranges for something to happen; usually by someone else. Its core meaning ranges over three English concepts: "to let/allow" (permission), "to have something done" (causation, arranging for a service), and "to leave (something as it is / in a place)". Structurally it behaves like a modal verb: it takes a bare infinitive (no "te") and forms a verb cluster at the end of the clause. Crucially, in the perfect tense "laten" does NOT use its past participle "gelaten" when combined with another infinitive; instead you get a double-infinitive construction ("heeft laten repareren", not "heeft laten gerepareerd"), a pattern shared with other verb-cluster verbs like "zien", "horen", "helpen". "Laten" also combines with reflexive "zich" to create passive-like meanings ("zich laten zien" = "to show up / let oneself be seen").

inseparable-prefixes.intro_tr: Dutch has a small set of verbal prefixes; be-, ver-, ont-, and her-; that are always inseparable: they never break away from the verb stem, are never stressed (the stress falls on the following syllable, e.g. beTALen, verKOpen), and never trigger the ge- prefix in the past participle. Unlike separable prefixes (op-, aan-, mee-, etc.), which are independent words that jump to the end of the clause, these four prefixes are permanently fused to the verb and behave more like a fixed part of the word's spelling and meaning. Each prefix carries its own semantic flavor: be- typically makes a verb transitive ('to do X to something directly'), ver- signals change, transformation, or 'doing wrongly/completely', ont- signals removal, escape, or a sudden beginning, and her- means 'again, re-'. Because these prefixes are so common (hundreds of everyday verbs use them), recognizing the pattern quickly tells you how to conjugate, stress, and form the participle correctly, and helps you guess the rough meaning of unfamiliar verbs.

participle-adjectives.title_tr: Participles Used as Adjectives (de gelezen krant)
participle-adjectives.intro_tr: Dutch present and past participles are not only used to build tenses like the perfect tense (heb gelezen); they can also work exactly like adjectives, placed directly in front of a noun or after zijn/worden. The present participle (stem + -end, e.g. lopend "walking") gives an active, ongoing meaning: the noun IS DOING the action. The past participle (ge- + stem + -d/-t, or an irregular form, e.g. gelezen "read") gives a passive or completed meaning: the noun HAS BEEN or WAS affected by the action. When used attributively (directly before a noun), participle-adjectives follow the same -e inflection rules as ordinary adjectives; in predicative position (after zijn/worden) they normally stay in their bare form. A few participle-adjectives have become so lexicalized that they can even take comparative and superlative endings, something true verbal participles cannot do.

word-order-inversion.intro_tr: Dutch is a strict V2 (verb-second) language: the finite (conjugated) verb must occupy the second position of a main clause, no matter what occupies the first position. In the default order the subject fills position 1 (Subject–Verb–Object), but when a speaker fronts something else; a time/place adverb, a direct object, a subordinate clause, a discourse particle, or a quoted sentence; for emphasis, topicalization, or simply because it is the logical starting point of the sentence, the subject is pushed to position 3 and the verb stays in position 2. This subject–verb swap is called "inversie" (inversion). Inversion is completely normal and frequent in Dutch; it is not a stylistic error but the grammatically required consequence of the V2 rule, and it is also the mechanism behind conditional clauses that drop "als" and behind reporting clauses that follow direct speech.

er-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Uses of er (Partitive er, Postponed Passive Subject)
er-advanced.intro_tr: Dutch "er" performs five separate grammatical jobs, and this page zooms in on the two most advanced ones: partitive (quantitative) "er", which stands in for a noun already mentioned when you go on to specify how many or how much of it there is, and postponed-subject "er", which fills the empty front position of a sentence (often passive) when the real grammatical subject is indefinite and has been pushed to the end of the clause. Both uses feel counterintuitive to English speakers because English simply drops the equivalent word ("I have two" vs. Dutch "Ik heb er twee"). Crucially, Dutch allows; and in careful style even expects; two adjacent "er"s when the existential and partitive functions overlap in the same clause ("Er zijn er nog drie"). Word order is strict in both uses: partitive "er" always precedes its quantifier, and postponed-subject "er" disappears the moment the indefinite subject is fronted or the sentence is rebuilt with a definite subject.

examples.target: Hoeveel appels heb je gekocht? Ik heb er zes gekocht.

examples.note_tr: 'er' must sit right after the finite verb 'heb', before the quantifier.

examples.target: Er wordt vanavond een feest gegeven.
examples.translation_tr: A party is being given tonight.
examples.note_tr: 'een feest' is the real, indefinite subject, postponed to the end; 'er' fills the empty front position.

examples.target: Er werden gisteren twee huizen verkocht.
examples.translation_tr: Two houses were sold yesterday.
examples.note_tr: Plural indefinite subject 'twee huizen' still triggers verb agreement (werden), even though it stands at the end.

examples.target: Ik weet dat er morgen een nieuwe wet wordt ingevoerd.
examples.translation_tr: I know that a new law will be introduced tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: In a subordinate clause the verb group moves to the end, but 'er' stays right after 'dat'.

examples.target: Er moet nog een besluit genomen worden.
examples.translation_tr: A decision still needs to be made.
examples.note_tr: 'er' co-occurs with a modal verb (moet) plus a passive infinitive construction (genomen worden).

relative-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic die/dat/waar system, Dutch has a set of advanced relative devices for special situations: wie for people without a specific noun antecedent ("whoever") or for people after a preposition, wat for indefinite pronouns, superlatives, and whole preceding clauses, hetgeen as its formal written equivalent, and waar+preposition compounds (waarmee, waarop, waarover...) that replace "preposition + dat" whenever the antecedent is a thing or idea. There is also a rare possessive relative wiens/wier ("whose"), mostly seen in formal or literary writing. Choosing correctly among these depends on what the antecedent is (person/thing/whole clause/nothing) and whether a preposition is involved.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of advanced relative pronouns
rows: replaces die when a preposition is needed
de vrouw aan wie ik het gaf
indefinite pronoun, superlative-as-noun, or whole clause
used instead of die/dat in these cases
de man wiens auto gestolen is

tables.caption_tr: Common waar + preposition combinations
rows: for which / in front of which
footnotes_tr: In spoken Dutch these compounds are often split, with the preposition moved to the end of the clause: 'het onderwerp waar we het over hadden' instead of 'waarover we het hadden'. The split form is common and neutral in speech but avoided in formal writing.

tables.caption_tr: When wat replaces die/dat
rows: Indefinite pronoun antecedent (iets, niets, alles, veel, weinig, wat)
Ik heb niets wat je kunt gebruiken.
het beste, het mooiste, het ergste
Dit is het mooiste wat ik ooit zag.
The whole preceding clause (no single noun antecedent)
Hij kwam te laat, wat me irriteerde.
Dat is het enige wat telt.

tables.caption_tr: wie vs. prepositional wie for people
rows: de man met wie ik sprak
waar + prep. used for a person
de man waar ik mee gesproken heb
Wie niet waagt, wie niet wint.
footnotes_tr: Using waar+prep for people (instead of prep.+wie) is widespread in casual speech but is generally corrected to 'prep. + wie' in writing and formal contexts.

tables.caption_tr: Possessive relative pronouns: wiens / wier
rows: de schrijver wiens boek bekroond werd
het bedrijf wiens... (usually rephrased with 'waarvan de')
de actrice wier film succesvol was
de kinderen wier ouders afwezig waren
footnotes_tr: wiens/wier sound old-fashioned and formal; in everyday speech 'van wie' is preferred: 'de schrijver van wie het boek bekroond werd'.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with advanced relative structures
rows: de man die ik het boek aan gaf
de man aan wie ik het boek gaf
A preposition referring to a person requires prep. + wie, never die directly after the preposition.
Indefinite pronoun antecedents (alles, iets, niets) always take wat, not die.
When the antecedent is the entire previous clause, use wat or hetgeen, not dat.
A concrete noun antecedent (de dag) needs waar+prep. or prep.+dat, not wat.
wiens used for a het-word without hesitation
wiens applied to neuter/thing antecedents is avoided; 'waarvan de' is the natural modern alternative.

examples.target: De man met wie ik gisteren sprak, is mijn buurman.
examples.translation_tr: The man with whom I spoke yesterday is my neighbor.
examples.note_tr: Preposition + wie is required for people; die cannot follow a preposition.

examples.target: Het bedrijf waarvoor ik werk, groeit snel.
examples.translation_tr: The company for which I work is growing fast.
examples.note_tr: waarvoor = voor + waar, used for things instead of 'voor dat'.

examples.target: Hij zei dat hij ziek was, wat niet waar bleek te zijn.
examples.translation_tr: He said he was sick, which turned out not to be true.
examples.note_tr: wat here refers back to the entire previous clause, not a single noun.

examples.target: Hij zei dat hij ziek was, hetgeen niet waar bleek te zijn.
examples.translation_tr: He said he was sick, which turned out not to be true.
examples.note_tr: hetgeen is the formal, written-register equivalent of clause-referring wat.

examples.target: Alles wat je nodig hebt, staat in dit boek.
examples.translation_tr: Everything you need is in this book.
examples.note_tr: Indefinite pronouns like alles, iets, niets always trigger wat, never dat/die.

examples.target: Wie het laatst lacht, lacht het best.
examples.translation_tr: Whoever laughs last, laughs best.
examples.note_tr: Headless wie meaning 'whoever'; no antecedent noun at all; a fixed proverb.

examples.target: De schrijfster wier nieuwe roman net verschenen is, wint een prijs.
examples.translation_tr: The (female) writer whose new novel has just appeared is winning a prize.
examples.note_tr: wier is the feminine/plural possessive relative pronoun; very formal, often avoided in speech.

examples.target: Dat is iets waarover ik lang heb nagedacht.
examples.translation_tr: That is something I've thought about for a long time.
examples.note_tr: waarover = over + waar; the two parts can also be split: waar ... over.

discourse-particles.title_tr: Discourse Particles (toch, wel, maar, eens, even)
discourse-particles.intro_tr: Dutch speakers constantly sprinkle small unstressed words; toch, wel, maar, eens, even, and combinations of them; into sentences to add attitude, emotion, or social tone without changing the factual content. Linguists call these modal or discourse particles, and they almost never translate into a single English word; instead they signal things like contradiction, reassurance, encouragement, casualness, or softness. They are unstressed and are placed right after the finite verb (and after any pronoun object) in the middle field of the clause, most commonly in imperatives and questions. Several particles frequently stack together (e.g. "kom eens even hier") to turn a blunt command into a friendly, low-pressure request. Because leaving them out often makes Dutch sound abrupt, cold, or overly formal, mastering these five words is one of the biggest steps toward sounding like a native speaker.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Five Core Discourse Particles
rows: Je komt toch? (You are coming, right?)
Contrastive emphasis, reassures or affirms against doubt/negative
Ik vind het wel leuk. (I do like it, actually.)
Softens commands/suggestions; also means 'just, only, merely'
Softens a request/imperative; casual invitation; also literal 'once'
Probeer het eens. (Just give it a try.)
Softens a request; implies briefness/small effort

tables.caption_tr: toch; Detailed Uses
rows: Contradicting a negative statement or belief
'It just doesn't work (despite what you thought/hoped).'
We hadden toch afgesproken om acht uur?
'We did agree on eight o'clock, remember?'

tables.caption_tr: wel; Detailed Uses
rows: 'I CAN do it' (contrary to what you might think)
Direct contrast with a preceding niet
Hij werkt niet, maar zij wel.
Emphasizing that something is in fact true
Het is wel duur, maar goed.

tables.caption_tr: maar; Detailed Uses
rows: Softening an imperative into a friendly suggestion
Je mag maar één stuk nemen.
Combined with eens for extra softness

tables.caption_tr: eens; Detailed Uses
rows: Combined with maar for gentle push

tables.caption_tr: even; Detailed Uses
rows: Softening a request (implies little effort needed)
Combined with eens for maximal softness
'Come take a quick look, would you?'
Downplaying the size/importance of a task
Ik moet nog even iets regelen.
'I just need to sort something out quickly.'

tables.caption_tr: Common Particle Combinations (Stacking)
rows: Maximally soft, casual request; 'come here for a sec, would you?'
Encouraging push to try, no risk implied
Heb je dat wel eens gedaan?
'Have you ever done that?' (wel eens = 'ever, on occasion')
Reassuring + brief; 'just wait a moment, it's fine'

tables.caption_tr: Word Order: Where Particles Go in the Sentence
rows: Right after the finite verb, before/after pronoun objects but before other complements
After the finite verb and subject
After the finite verb and subject, before the rest
Placed before the final verb cluster, after the subject
...dat hij het toch wel gedaan heeft.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes for English Speakers
rows: 'maar' is also a softening/limiting particle unrelated to contrast
Doe het maar = 'Go ahead and do it', not 'but do it'
'eens' is very often a softening particle with no counting meaning
Kijk eens = 'Take a look', not 'Look one time'
Sentences can sound blunt, cold, or robotic without them
Add toch/wel/maar/eens/even to soften tone in requests and imperatives
Placing the particle at the very end of the sentence
Particles belong in the middle field, right after the finite verb/pronoun
Zeg het maar niet, not Zeg het niet maar
Stacking too many particles at once in careful/formal writing
Heavy stacking (eens even maar) sounds overly casual/spoken, awkward in formal text
Use at most one or two particles in formal writing

examples.target: Doe het toch!
examples.translation_tr: Just do it (already)!; insisting, mild impatience
examples.note_tr: toch here pushes the listener toward an action they are hesitating about

examples.target: Dat is toch niet zo moeilijk?
examples.translation_tr: That's not that hard, is it?; seeking agreement/confirmation
examples.note_tr: toch turns a statement into a soft tag question

examples.target: Ik heb het wel gedaan.
examples.translation_tr: I did do it (contrary to what you assumed); contrastive emphasis
examples.note_tr: wel contradicts an implied or stated negative expectation

examples.target: Kom je wel?
examples.translation_tr: Are you actually coming?; checking/reassurance
examples.note_tr: wel here signals mild worry that the answer might be no

examples.target: Ga maar zitten.
examples.translation_tr: Go ahead and sit down.; friendly permission/invitation
examples.note_tr: maar softens an imperative into a relaxed suggestion

examples.target: Het is maar een grapje.
examples.translation_tr: It's just a joke.; minimizing/downplaying
examples.note_tr: maar here means 'only, merely'

examples.target: Kijk eens!
examples.translation_tr: Look at this!; casual, inviting attention
examples.note_tr: eens softens the imperative and makes it sound friendly rather than blunt

examples.target: Kom eens even hier.
examples.translation_tr: Come here for a sec, would you?; combined softening particles
examples.note_tr: eens and even stack to make the request as gentle and casual as possible

comparative-clauses.intro_tr: Dutch has three distinct comparative-clause tools that beginners often confuse: "hoe...hoe" (the...the, expressing parallel increase/decrease), "alsof" (as if, introducing a hypothetical or pretended comparison), and "zoals" (as/like, introducing a real comparison, example, or manner). Each triggers a different word order and mood nuance. "Hoe...hoe" pairs two comparative forms across two clauses that both use subordinate (verb-final) word order. "Alsof" introduces a subordinate clause and often pairs with a past tense to signal something unreal, much like the English "as if I were". "Zoals" introduces either a full clause (meaning "as") or a short list/example (meaning "such as" or "like"), and only triggers verb-final order when a full clause follows.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: the three comparative structures at a glance
rows: a noun phrase or short example list

tables.caption_tr: hoe...hoe: formation rules
rows: Start each clause with 'hoe' + a comparative form (adjective/adverb in -er, or meer/minder + adjective).
Keep the finite verb at the very end of each clause (subordinate-style order), even in the second clause which is grammatically the main clause.
Hoe meer hij eet, hoe dikker hij wordt.
Irregular comparatives (goed→beter, veel→meer, weinig→minder) are used exactly as in normal comparative sentences.
Hoe meer, hoe beter. / Hoe minder, hoe liever.
A comma always separates the two 'hoe' clauses.
Hoe ouder je wordt, hoe wijzer je wordt.
Both clauses must contain a comparative element; you cannot leave one clause in the positive (base) form.
✗ Hoe meer je leest, hoe je slim wordt. (wrong) → ✓ ...hoe slimmer je wordt.

tables.caption_tr: alsof: usage and mood
rows: the subject fakes a state that is not true
Hij doet alsof hij ziek is.
similar to English 'as if I were' (irrealis)
Ze praat alsof ze de baas was.
comparison to something that did not actually happen before
Hij keek alsof er niets gebeurd was.
finite verb / verb cluster moves to clause-final position

tables.caption_tr: zoals: three main uses
rows: Zoals je ziet, is het klaar.
triggers verb-final order if a clause follows
Hij zingt zoals zijn moeder zong.

tables.caption_tr: Common confusions: als vs zoals vs alsof vs hoe
rows: if / when / as (comparison of equality: zo...als)
Hij is zo groot als zijn vader. (as...as)
as / such as / like (real comparison or example)
using 'als' instead of 'zoals' before an example list
Groenten, zoals wortels en erwten. (NOT: als wortels)
as if / as though (hypothetical, often unreal)
using 'zoals' instead of 'alsof' for pretend/hypothetical comparisons
Hij doet alsof hij rijk is. (NOT: doet zoals hij rijk is)
Hoe eerder, hoe beter. (NOT: Hoe vroeg, hoe goed)

examples.target: Hoe meer je oefent, hoe beter je wordt.
examples.translation_tr: The more you practice, the better you get.
examples.note_tr: Both clauses use verb-final (subordinate-style) word order, even though the second 'hoe' clause is technically the main clause.

examples.target: Hoe ouder hij wordt, hoe koppiger hij wordt.
examples.translation_tr: The older he gets, the more stubborn he becomes.
examples.note_tr: Comparative adjectives (ouder, koppiger) immediately follow 'hoe' in each clause.

examples.target: Hij doet alsof hij niets gehoord heeft.
examples.translation_tr: He acts as if he heard nothing.
examples.note_tr: 'Alsof' introduces a subordinate clause with the finite verb pushed to the end (or perfect auxiliary + participle cluster).

examples.target: Ze keek me aan alsof ik gek was.
examples.translation_tr: She looked at me as if I were crazy.
examples.note_tr: Past tense after 'alsof' often expresses something unreal or hypothetical, similar to an English subjunctive 'were'.

examples.target: Doe niet alsof je me niet kent!
examples.translation_tr: Don't act as if you don't know me!
examples.note_tr: 'Alsof' clauses are very common after doen (alsof) meaning 'to pretend that'.

examples.target: Zoals je weet, begint de vergadering om negen uur.
examples.translation_tr: As you know, the meeting starts at nine o'clock.
examples.note_tr: Here 'zoals' introduces a full clause meaning 'as' and also has verb-final word order.

examples.target: Ik hou van fruit, zoals appels en peren.
examples.translation_tr: I like fruit, such as apples and pears.
examples.note_tr: 'Zoals' before a list of nouns means 'such as' / 'like' and does not require verb-final order because no clause follows.

examples.target: Hij speelt gitaar zoals zijn vader dat vroeger deed.
examples.translation_tr: He plays guitar the way his father used to.
examples.note_tr: 'Zoals' can compare an action to a similar past or hypothetical action performed by someone else.

nominalization.title_tr: Nominalization: het + Infinitive and the -ing Suffix
nominalization.intro_tr: Dutch has two productive ways to turn a verb into a noun. The first, het + infinitive (e.g., het lezen, het zwemmen), is fully productive; almost any verb can be turned into a neuter, singular-only noun that names the activity itself, much like the English gerund "reading" or "swimming." The second, the -ing suffix (e.g., wandeling, vergadering, opleiding), is only available for a limited, lexicalized set of verbs and produces a feminine (de-word) noun that can be pluralized and usually names a concrete instance, result, or institution rather than the abstract activity. Because both strategies can apply to the same verb with different meanings (het lezen "the act of reading" vs. de lezing "a lecture"), learners must memorize -ing nouns individually rather than assume they always exist. Note on pronunciation: this topic is about spelling and word formation, not sound changes; no special phonetic notation is needed here.

tables.caption_tr: Forming het + Infinitive Nouns (fully productive)
rows: Any infinitive can be nominalized this way
Can drift toward meaning 'food' in context
Contrast with de wandeling, a walk
Very common in signs/rules: het roken is verboden
Object needs 'van': het leren van talen
footnotes_tr: The bare infinitive without 'het' (e.g., Roken is ongezond) is used for general, timeless statements; 'het + infinitive' is used when referring to a specific, definite instance of the activity.

tables.caption_tr: Forming -ing Nouns from Verbs (limited, lexicalized set); spelling rules
footnotes_tr: The spelling changes follow the same open/closed syllable rules used everywhere in Dutch: long vowels written double only in closed syllables, single in open syllables; short vowels require a doubled following consonant to stay closed.

tables.caption_tr: het + Infinitive vs. -ing Noun: Key Grammatical Differences
rows: the action or activity itself, ongoing/generic
a concrete instance, result, or institution
fully productive; works for virtually any verb
not productive; only a fixed, lexicalized set of verbs
needs 'van': het lezen van het boek
often used without needing 'van' as a full independent noun

tables.caption_tr: Meaning Shifts: Same Verb, Two Different Nouns
footnotes_tr: These pairs show that -ing nouns are not simply 'the same meaning with a different article'; they frequently develop their own specialized, lexicalized sense.

tables.caption_tr: Common Time/Manner Phrases with het + Infinitive
rows: met het schrijven van het boek
with the writing of the book
footnotes_tr: This construction is the standard way to translate an English '-ing' clause introduced by a preposition (while cooking, after swimming, etc.); English '-ing' here is NOT translated with the Dutch -ing suffix.

examples.target: Het roken is hier verboden.
examples.translation_tr: Smoking is forbidden here.
examples.note_tr: 'het roken' = the (specific, definite) act of smoking in this place.

examples.target: Zwemmen is goed voor je gezondheid.
examples.translation_tr: Swimming is good for your health.
examples.note_tr: Bare infinitive used as a generic subject noun; no article needed for general statements.

examples.target: Na het eten gaan we wandelen.
examples.translation_tr: After eating, we're going for a walk.
examples.note_tr: 'na het + infinitive' = 'after -ing', a very common time-clause pattern.

examples.target: De vergadering begint om tien uur.
examples.translation_tr: The meeting starts at ten o'clock.
examples.note_tr: 'de vergadering' (the -ing noun) refers to one specific, concrete meeting event, unlike 'het vergaderen' (the general activity of meeting).

examples.target: Hij volgt een opleiding tot leraar.
examples.translation_tr: He is doing a training program to become a teacher.
examples.note_tr: 'opleiding' is a lexicalized -ing noun meaning 'course/training program', not just 'the act of training'.

examples.target: Tijdens het lezen viel ze in slaap.
examples.translation_tr: While reading, she fell asleep.
examples.note_tr: 'tijdens het + infinitive' = 'while/during -ing'.

examples.target: De lezing over klimaatverandering was interessant.
examples.translation_tr: The lecture about climate change was interesting.
examples.note_tr: 'lezing' looks related to 'lezen' (to read) but has drifted in meaning to 'a lecture/talk', not 'reading'.

examples.target: Het leren van een nieuwe taal kost tijd.
examples.translation_tr: Learning a new language takes time.
examples.note_tr: 'het leren van X' is the standard way to say '-ing X' as a noun phrase; the object needs 'van' since infinitives-as-nouns can't take a direct object directly.

men-formal-subjects.title_tr: The General Subject men and the Formal Pronoun u
men-formal-subjects.intro_tr: Dutch has two related but distinct tools for talking about people in a general or formal way: the indefinite pronoun men ('one', 'people', 'you' in general statements) and the formal second-person pronoun u ('you', polite). Grammatically, both are treated as third-person singular, so they always combine with the same verb form as hij/zij (men zegt, u zegt; never men zeggen or u zegt niet as *u zeggen*). Men is mainly found in written, official, or somewhat old-fashioned formal Dutch, and is increasingly replaced in speech by je/jij, iedereen, or the impersonal passive (er wordt...). U, by contrast, remains very much alive in everyday formal speech: it is used to address strangers, elders, authority figures, customers, or anyone you want to show respect or social distance to, and it has its own possessive (uw) and reflexive (u/zich) forms distinct from informal je/jij.

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation with men; always the 3rd person singular verb form
rows: One says that... / People say that...
Men heeft het recht om te stemmen.
One has the right to vote.
One is not allowed to smoke here.

tables.caption_tr: u vs. jij/je; full pronoun comparison
Strategies for expressing a general, unspecified subject
rows: Men zegt dat het gaat regenen.
Informal, very common in everyday spoken Dutch
Iedereen weet dat roken ongezond is.
impersonal passive: er wordt + past participle
Common on official signs and in formal notices
Ze zeggen dat het gaat regenen.
Colloquial, vague reference to unnamed people

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with men
rows: It is said that... / They say that...
Men neme... (archaic imperative, used in recipes)
Please be so kind as to... (very formal request)

tables.caption_tr: When to use u; formality contexts
rows: Addressing a stranger or older person
Wij verzoeken u dit formulier in te vullen.
Talking to close friends or family
Dames en heren, mag ik uw aandacht?

examples.target: Men zegt dat het weer gaat veranderen.
examples.translation_tr: They say that the weather is going to change.
examples.note_tr: 'Men' + 3rd person singular verb form 'zegt' (from zeggen).

examples.target: Hier mag men niet roken.
examples.translation_tr: Smoking is not allowed here.
examples.note_tr: Literally 'One may not smoke here'; typical on official signs.

examples.target: Kunt u mij vertellen hoe laat het is?
examples.translation_tr: Could you tell me what time it is?
examples.note_tr: Formal 'u' used when addressing a stranger.

examples.target: Wij danken u voor uw begrip.
examples.translation_tr: We thank you for your understanding.
examples.note_tr: 'u' as object, 'uw' as possessive; typical formal closing in letters/emails.

examples.target: Men moet altijd de regels volgen.
examples.translation_tr: One must always follow the rules.
examples.note_tr: 'Men' with modal verb 'moet'; still 3rd person singular form.

examples.target: Heeft u al besloten wat u wilt bestellen?
examples.translation_tr: Have you already decided what you would like to order?
examples.note_tr: Typical formal service-industry question, e.g. by a waiter.

examples.target: Zoals men weet, is Nederland een klein land.
examples.translation_tr: As is well known, the Netherlands is a small country.
examples.note_tr: Fixed formal phrase 'zoals men weet' = 'as is well known'.

examples.target: Wilt u uw jas even ophangen?
examples.translation_tr: Would you like to hang up your coat?
examples.note_tr: Polite request using 'u' and possessive 'uw'.

preposition-nuance.title_tr: Fine-Grained Preposition Distinctions (op / aan / bij / tegen)
preposition-nuance.intro_tr: The four prepositions op, aan, bij, and tegen all get translated into English as "on," "at," "near," or "against," which is exactly why they are a classic trap for English speakers: English lets one word (like "on") cover many Dutch situations that Dutch splits apart based on the physical or logical relationship between the objects. In short, op marks contact with a surface from above (gravity holds it there), aan marks attachment or connection to something (often vertical, or a fixed point), bij marks general proximity or "being at someone's location," and tegen marks contact combined with pressure, or opposition (physical or of opinion). These four also have large sets of fixed idiomatic expressions that do not follow the spatial logic at all and simply have to be memorized. This page organizes the spatial logic first, then time uses, then idioms, and finally a "typical English-speaker mistake" table to help you self-correct.

tables.caption_tr: Core spatial/logical meaning of op, aan, bij, tegen
rows: Resting ON TOP of a (usually horizontal) surface; contact caused by gravity
De kat ligt op het bed. (The cat is lying on the bed.)
Attached to, connected to, or right at the edge of something (often vertical or a fixed point)
De jas hangt aan de kapstok. (The coat hangs on the coat rack.)
In the general vicinity of, or at a person's/place's location
Ik woon bij het park. (I live near the park.)
Physical contact combined with pressure/leaning, OR opposition (physical or of opinion)
De ladder staat tegen de muur. (The ladder is standing against the wall.)

tables.caption_tr: op vs. aan: the classic 'surface contact' distinction
rows: Object resting flat on a horizontal surface
op de tafel, op de grond, op het bed
Gravity holds the object down onto a surface.
Object hanging/fixed on a vertical surface or point
aan de muur, aan het plafond, aan de haak
The object is attached/suspended, not resting on top.
Streets, islands, and many institutional locations
op straat, op het eiland, op kantoor, op school, op de universiteit
Idiomatic/institutional use of op that does not literally mean 'on top of'.
Edges, borders, coastlines, bodies of water
aan zee, aan de kust, aan het water, aan de rivier
aan marks location right at the edge/border of something.
Fixed idiom; not op tafel, which would mean literally on top of the table surface.

tables.caption_tr: bij vs. tegen: proximity vs. contact/opposition
rows: Near a place or object (not touching it)
bij het station, bij de deur, bij de winkel
General proximity, no physical contact implied.
At someone's home, workplace, or in someone's care
bij de dokter, bij mij thuis, bij mijn ouders
tegen de muur leunen, tegen de deur duwen
Physical contact plus force/pressure, unlike bij which has no contact.
Opposing an opinion, plan, or team
tegen dit plan zijn, tegen elkaar spelen
Abstract 'against' -- opposition of stance or competition.
tegen marks the addressee when reporting speech, distinct from aan in some contexts (aan iemand schrijven = to write to someone).

tables.caption_tr: Time expressions with op, aan, bij, tegen
rows: Exact days, dates, and points in time
op maandag, op 3 mei, op tijd
Used for calendar-specific or precise timing.
Marks the start/end portion of a period (fixed phrases only)
aan het begin van de week, aan het einde van de dag
Not freely productive; limited to set phrases.
During/at the occasion of an event
tegen de avond, tegen drieën, tegen het einde van de maand
Unlike op, tegen signals approximation, not an exact point.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed idiomatic expressions by preposition
rows: at work / working (also used with aan het + infinitive continuous)
by way of / as a form of

tables.caption_tr: Frequent mistakes English speakers make with these four prepositions
rows: Institutions like school/work/university idiomatically take op, not bij.
op de muur would suggest something painted/sprayed directly on the surface, not hung on it.
Fixed idiom for sitting down to eat; op tafel means literally on top of the table's surface.

examples.note_tr: tegen also expresses opposition of opinion, not just physical contact.

negation-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic niet/geen system, Dutch has a set of more formal, emphatic, or literary negation words that native speakers use to add nuance; hardly (nauwelijks), by no means (geenszins), not... either in formal register (evenmin), and not in the least (allerminst). These words behave grammatically like adverbs and slot into normal V2 word order, but each carries its own register (some are neutral, some distinctly formal/written) and its own typical collocations. Because Dutch avoids stacking two plain negative particles in the same clause, these words also serve as elegant substitutes for repeating 'niet' or 'geen'. This page collects the core advanced negators, their exact meanings, where they sit in the sentence, and the mistakes learners most often make when moving from basic to advanced negation.
