examples.note_tr: laat staan is an idiomatic negative-intensifying expression meaning 'let alone'.

examples.translation_tr: He is far from satisfied with the result.
examples.note_tr: verre van + adjective is a fixed way of expressing strong negation without using niet or geen.

triple-verb-clusters.title_tr: Triple Verb Clusters (zou hebben kunnen doen)
triple-verb-clusters.intro_tr: A "triple verb cluster" is a chain of three (sometimes effectively four, if you count zou) verb forms stacked together at the end of a clause, most famously in the pattern zou + hebben/zijn + modal + main-verb-infinitive (e.g. zou hebben kunnen doen, "would have been able to do"). This construction combines the conditional (zou), the perfect auxiliary (hebben/zijn), and a modal verb (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen) with a main verb. The key grammatical trick is the Infinitivus Pro Participio (IPP) rule, also called the "double infinitive" effect: when a modal verb is combined with hebben/zijn and another infinitive, the modal itself surfaces as a bare infinitive (kunnen) instead of its normal past participle (gekund). Word order at the end of the clause can vary; the most common "green" order is aux-modal-infinitive (hebben kunnen doen), but a modal-aux-participle order (kunnen hebben gedaan) also exists and often carries a different meaning: ability/counterfactual capacity versus epistemic possibility ("might have"). Since pronunciation of these long clusters follows normal Dutch spelling and stress rules with no special phonetic notation, no reading transcription is given below.

examples.target: Hij zou het kunnen hebben gedaan, we weten het niet zeker.
examples.translation_tr: He might have done it, we don't know for sure.
examples.note_tr: Epistemic reading: modal-aux-participle order (kunnen hebben gedaan) expresses speculation, not ability.

examples.target: Jullie zouden eerder hebben moeten vertrekken.
examples.translation_tr: You (plural) should have left earlier.
examples.note_tr: vertrekken normally takes zijn in the perfect, but after a modal the whole cluster commonly reverts to hebben.

examples.target: Zonder jouw hulp zou ik het nooit hebben kunnen doen.
examples.translation_tr: Without your help, I would never have been able to do it.
examples.note_tr: The object (het) and adverb (nooit) sit before the verb cluster, never inside it.

examples.target: Hij zou eerder zijn kunnen gaan als het niet had geregend.
examples.translation_tr: He would have been able to leave earlier if it hadn't rained.
examples.note_tr: gaan is a motion verb, so the perfect auxiliary inside the cluster is zijn, not hebben.

examples.target: Ik denk dat hij het wel had kunnen weten.
examples.translation_tr: I think he could well have known that.
examples.note_tr: The same triple-cluster pattern (aux-modal-infinitive) also appears in the plain pluperfect, without zou.

impersonal-passive.intro_tr: The impersonal passive (onpersoonlijk passief) turns an intransitive verb; one with no direct object, such as dansen, werken, or lachen; into a passive construction that has no real grammatical subject at all. Since Dutch main clauses normally require a subject in first position, the dummy word "er" fills that empty slot: "Er wordt gedanst" literally means "It is being danced," but is best translated as "There is dancing" or "People are dancing." It is built exactly like the ordinary passive, with worden (or zijn in the perfect tenses) plus the past participle, and it expresses a general, agentless activity rather than describing what happens to a specific object. When another element; usually a time or place expression; occupies the front position of the sentence, "er" moves to the slot right after the finite verb, and in written or formal style it can often be dropped altogether, though keeping it sounds more natural in everyday speech.

examples.note_tr: Simple past tense: werd + past participle.

examples.target: Hier wordt niet gerookt.

examples.translation_tr: There was a long silence about that topic yesterday.

examples.target: Er moet nu hard gewerkt worden, niet gepraat.

modality-nuance.title_tr: Modality Nuances: schijnen, blijken, lijken, horen te
modality-nuance.intro_tr: Dutch has four verbs that let a speaker signal exactly *how* they know something, or how strongly something is expected; a nuance English often leaves to context or modal adverbs. **Schijnen** reports hearsay ("apparently, I heard/it's said that..."), **blijken** reports something confirmed by evidence or facts that came to light ("it turns out that..."), **lijken** reports a subjective impression from perception ("it seems, it looks like..."), and **horen te** expresses a soft social or normative expectation ("is supposed to, ought to"), weaker than the hard obligation of **moeten**. All four typically combine with **te + infinitive**, unlike the core modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen), which take a bare infinitive. Mastering these verbs is essential for expressing evidentiality and mild obligation with native-like precision at an advanced level.

subjunctive-remnants.title_tr: Fossilized Subjunctive (leve, moge, het zij zo)
subjunctive-remnants.intro_tr: Dutch once had a fully productive subjunctive mood (de aanvoegende wijs), used for wishes, hypotheticals, and formal commands, much like German still does today. In Modern Dutch this mood has essentially died out and survives only as isolated, unproductive "fossils"; fixed phrases frozen in time that native speakers learn as whole chunks rather than by applying a living grammatical rule. You will meet these fossils in toasts and exclamations (leve!), blessings and wishes (moge, God zegene je), legal/ceremonial oaths, proverbs, and elevated literary or biblical style. The hallmark of the fossilized subjunctive is a verb form built on the bare stem with an -e ending, used regardless of the normal 3rd-person -t rule of the present tense (compare leve vs. the regular leeft). Because these forms are no longer generated freely, the best approach is to memorize the fixed expressions as vocabulary items rather than trying to conjugate a "Dutch subjunctive" yourself; modern Dutch expresses wishes, hopes, and hypotheticals with hopelijk, mogen + infinitive, or the conditional zou instead.

te-infinitive-advanced.title_tr: Advanced te + Infinitive Constructions (alvorens te, zonder te)
te-infinitive-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic 'om te + infinitive' purpose clause, written and formal Dutch uses a family of prepositional connectors; 'zonder te' (without doing), 'door te' (by doing), 'in plaats van te' (instead of doing), and the literary 'alvorens te' (before doing); that all link two actions sharing the same subject via 'te' + infinitive. A special extra layer is the perfect te-infinitive ('na te hebben/zijn' + past participle), used when the linked action happened earlier than the main-clause action. The single hard rule to remember: these te-constructions only work when both clauses share the same subject; the moment the subjects differ, Dutch switches to a full subordinate clause with 'dat' (zonder dat, in plaats van dat) or a plain conjunction (voordat). 'Alvorens' is markedly formal/literary and is largely restricted to written registers; in speech, 'voordat' is the everyday equivalent.

tables.caption_tr: Core prepositional te + infinitive connectors
rows: Hij spaart om een auto te kopen.
Je leert Nederlands door veel te lezen.
In plaats van te klagen, hielp hij mee.
Alvorens te antwoorden, dacht hij na.
with a view to (noun, not te+inf)
Met het oog op de kosten, wachtten ze.
footnotes_tr: All of these require the subject of the te-infinitive action to be identical to the subject of the main clause.

tables.caption_tr: Perfect (past) te-infinitive: na te hebben/zijn + past participle
rows: Na het boek te hebben gelezen, gaf hij het terug.
Na aangekomen te zijn, belde hij haar meteen.
Hij vertrok zonder afscheid te hebben genomen.
Alvorens vertrokken te zijn, belde hij nog even.
footnotes_tr: The auxiliary in these constructions (hebben/zijn) stays in the infinitive form; it is never conjugated.
Used mainly in written, narrative, or formal registers; spoken Dutch usually prefers 'nadat' + a full clause.

tables.caption_tr: alvorens vs. voordat vs. eer: formality comparison
rows: Alvorens te vertrekken, sloot hij de deur.
can also head a full subordinate clause
Alvorens hij vertrok, sloot hij de deur.
Voordat hij vertrok, sloot hij de deur.
Eer hij vertrok, nam hij afscheid.
footnotes_tr: In spoken and everyday written Dutch, 'voordat' (or simply 'voor') is by far the most common choice; 'alvorens' and 'eer' mark a text as formal or literary.

tables.caption_tr: Subject-identity rule: te-infinitive vs. dat-clause
rows: Hij ging weg zonder te betalen.
Hij ging weg zonder dat iemand het merkte.
Zij vertrok zonder afscheid te nemen.
Zij vertrok zonder dat wij het wisten.
In plaats van te klagen, hielp hij mee.
In plaats van dat hij klaagde, hielp hij mee.
Alvorens te antwoorden, dacht hij na.
Alvorens hij antwoordde, dacht hij na. (own subject, no 'te', no 'dat')
footnotes_tr: Note that 'alvorens' never combines with 'dat'; when the subjects differ, 'alvorens' simply introduces a normal subordinate clause without 'te'.
For purpose clauses with different subjects, Dutch uses 'zodat' or 'opdat' instead of 'om ... dat'.

tables.caption_tr: Word order: te-infinitive clause placement
rows: Zonder te aarzelen, tekende zij het document.
Zij tekende het document zonder te aarzelen.
[Na ... te hebben + participle], + finite verb + subject
Na het contract te hebben gelezen, tekende zij het.
footnotes_tr: When the te-infinitive clause is placed first, it counts as the first sentence position, so the main clause verb must directly follow it (verb-second/V2 rule); this often produces an inverted subject-verb order in the main clause.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes
rows: Alvorens hij vertrok, belde hij. / Voordat hij vertrok, belde hij.
The auxiliary after 'te' must stay in the infinitive ('hebben'), never conjugated ('heeft').
Hij vertrok zonder te hebben gegroet.
*Zij vertrok zonder te dat wij het wisten.
'zonder te' and 'zonder dat' cannot be mixed; different subjects require plain 'zonder dat'.
Zij vertrok zonder dat wij het wisten.
*Om te slagen hij moet hard studeren.
A fronted te-clause triggers subject-verb inversion in the main clause (V2 rule).
Om te slagen, moet hij hard studeren.

examples.target: Alvorens te vertrekken, controleerde hij alle deuren en ramen.
examples.translation_tr: Before leaving, he checked all the doors and windows.
examples.note_tr: 'alvorens te + infinitive' requires the same subject in both parts of the sentence; it is a formal/literary alternative to 'voordat hij vertrok'.

examples.target: Zonder ook maar iets te zeggen, liep ze de kamer uit.
examples.translation_tr: Without saying anything at all, she walked out of the room.

examples.target: Je kunt deze taal leren door elke dag te oefenen.
examples.translation_tr: You can learn this language by practicing every day.
examples.note_tr: 'door te + infinitive' expresses the means/method by which something is achieved.

examples.target: In plaats van te klagen, zou je een oplossing moeten zoeken.
examples.translation_tr: Instead of complaining, you should look for a solution.

examples.target: Na het rapport te hebben gelezen, belde de directeur meteen zijn advocaat.
examples.translation_tr: After having read the report, the director immediately called his lawyer.
examples.note_tr: This is a perfect te-infinitive: 'na te hebben' + past participle, used when the subordinate action happened before the main-clause action.

examples.target: Hij ondertekende het contract zonder de kleine lettertjes te hebben gelezen.
examples.translation_tr: He signed the contract without having read the fine print.
examples.note_tr: Note 'te hebben gelezen', not a conjugated 'heeft'; the infinitive 'hebben' stays uninflected.

examples.target: Alvorens een besluit te nemen, wil de commissie alle feiten kennen.
examples.translation_tr: Before making a decision, the committee wants to know all the facts.

examples.target: Zonder dat iemand het merkte, verliet hij stilletjes het feest.
examples.translation_tr: Without anyone noticing, he quietly left the party.
examples.note_tr: Because the subject of the subordinate action (iemand) differs from the subject of the main clause (hij), 'zonder te' is impossible here; 'zonder dat' + a full clause must be used instead.

fronting-topicalization.intro_tr: In Dutch, the finite verb must always stay in second position (the V2 rule), but the slot before it; position 1; is flexible: almost any single constituent (a time/place adverbial, a direct or prepositional object, a predicate adjective, or even a whole subordinate clause) can be moved there instead of the subject. This is called fronting or topicalization, and it always forces subject–verb inversion (the subject moves to right after the verb). Fronting is not just decorative word order; it organizes the sentence into a topic (what the sentence is 'about', usually given/known information) and a comment (the new information, which Dutch tends to push toward the end of the clause, the 'end-focus' principle). English speakers often get this wrong in two ways: forgetting to invert after a fronted adverbial ("Gisteren ik zag hem" is wrong), and reaching for English strategies like passive voice or cleft sentences ("It was him that...") where Dutch simply fronts the element and inverts. Only one constituent may occupy position 1; you cannot front two things at once.

tables.caption_tr: The basic pattern: neutral order vs. fronted order
footnotes_tr: Whatever fills position 1, the subject always moves to the slot immediately after the finite verb; this is obligatory, not optional.

tables.caption_tr: What can be fronted, and what it signals
rows: Vorig jaar woonde ik in Utrecht.
Neutral scene-setting; extremely common and stylistically unmarked
Orients the listener spatially before introducing new information
Langzaam liep hij naar de deur.
Die film heb ik al gezien.
Marks the object as given/topic, or creates contrast
Aan hem heb ik niets te danken.
Foregrounds a person or thing already under discussion
Moe was hij wel, maar tevreden.
Omdat het regende, bleven we thuis.
Sets up a cause/condition/time frame as background before the main point
Highly marked, emphatic, mostly written/rhetorical style

tables.caption_tr: Discourse functions of fronting (why Dutch speakers choose it)
rows: Repeats or refers to something already mentioned, keeping it as the sentence's starting point
Ik kocht een fiets. Die fiets heb ik nu al drie jaar.
Sets one element against an implied alternative
IK heb het niet gedaan; hij wel.
Establishes time or place before presenting the main event
In 1998 verhuisde het gezin naar Rotterdam.
Old/known information goes first (position 1), brand-new information is saved for the end of the clause
Dat probleem heeft de regering gisteren eindelijk opgelost.

tables.caption_tr: Dutch fronting vs. equivalent English strategies
rows: Dat boek heb ik al gelezen.
Fronting without inversion, or plain statement
That book, I've already read. / I've already read that book.
Front adverbial, push indefinite subject after verb (often with 'er')
Er komt een man het huis binnen.
A man comes into the house. / There comes a man into the house.
Fronting alone is usually enough; no special construction needed
It was him (that) I saw yesterday.
Front the whole subordinate clause, invert main clause
Toen hij aankwam, begon het te regenen.
Same clause order, but no inversion required
When he arrived, it began to rain.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes for English-speaking learners
rows: Forgetting inversion after a fronted element
English keeps SVO after fronting ('Yesterday I saw him'); Dutch always inverts subject and verb after anything in position 1.
Gisteren in het park ik zag hem.
Gisteren zag ik hem in het park. / In het park zag ik hem gisteren.
Only ONE constituent may occupy position 1; extra elements stay in their normal post-verbal slots.
Wat betreft dit boek, ik heb het gelezen.
Dutch usually prefers direct fronting over an explicit 'as for' phrase, which sounds heavy/formal in comparison.
Treating fronting as optional stylistic decoration only
Always defaulting to subject-first order even when referring back to known information
Front the already-mentioned element to keep topic continuity: 'Die auto heeft hij net gekocht.'
Native Dutch strongly prefers starting from given information rather than always starting with the subject.
Forgetting 'er' when subject becomes indefinite and moves after the verb
In de kamer stond een man. / Er stond een man in de kamer.
An indefinite subject displaced from position 1 often needs 'er' to fill the empty subject slot or precede it naturally; this interacts with the general rules of 'er'.

examples.target: Dit boek heb ik nog niet gelezen.
examples.translation_tr: This book, I haven't read yet. (fronted direct object, linking back to something already mentioned)

examples.target: Morgen ga ik naar Amsterdam.
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow I'm going to Amsterdam. (fronted time adverbial; very common, neutral topicalization)

examples.target: Aan die vraag heb ik nog niet gedacht.
examples.translation_tr: I haven't thought about that question yet. (fronted prepositional object 'aan die vraag')

examples.target: Blij was ze niet met het resultaat.
examples.translation_tr: She was not happy with the result. (fronted predicate adjective for contrastive emphasis)

examples.target: Toen de regen begon, gingen we naar binnen.
examples.translation_tr: When the rain started, we went inside. (whole subordinate clause fills position 1, forcing inversion in the main clause)

examples.target: Hem kende ik al jaren.
examples.translation_tr: Him, I had known for years. (contrastive object fronting, implies 'unlike someone else')

examples.target: Zulke fouten maakt hij nooit.
examples.translation_tr: Such mistakes he never makes. (fronted object for emphasis, closer to English fronting but Dutch still inverts subject/verb)

examples.target: Op die stoel heeft niemand ooit gezeten.
examples.translation_tr: Nobody has ever sat on that chair. (fronted place PP with an indefinite subject 'niemand' appearing after the verb)

cleft-sentences.intro_tr: A cleft sentence splits a normal, single-clause sentence into two parts in order to place very strong emphasis on one specific piece of information; the focused element. The Dutch pattern is "Het is/zijn + [focused element] + die/dat/wat + [rest of the sentence]", where the choice between die, dat, and wat depends on the gender, number, and type of the focused noun, exactly as with ordinary relative pronouns. The verb "zijn" must agree in number with the focused element (is for singular, zijn for plural) and in tense with the rest of the sentence (is → was → zal zijn). Cleft sentences are especially common in spoken Dutch to correct, contrast, or highlight information ("not X, but Y"), and in questions asking specifically about the emphasized element. Since Dutch is written in the Latin alphabet with no separate phonetic transcription system, no special pronunciation notation is needed here; just read the words as spelled.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure of Cleft Sentences
rows: Het is Jan die dat gezegd heeft.
Het zijn de kinderen die spelen.
Het is de auto die kapot is.
Het is het boek dat ik lees.
Het zijn de boeken die ik lees.

tables.caption_tr: Choosing die, dat, or wat
rows: Standard choice for common-gender nouns and people
Always die, regardless of the noun's gender
Used when the focus is an entire idea rather than a concrete noun
Used after indefinite pronouns as focus
Superlative used as a noun (het beste, het mooiste)
e.g. Het is het beste wat je kunt doen.

tables.caption_tr: Tense Agreement: het is vs het was
rows: Het is Marie geweest die kookte.
Het zal Marie zijn die kookt.

tables.caption_tr: Cleft Sentence vs Neutral Word Order (Emphasis Comparison)
rows: Het is Jan die dat gezegd heeft.
Het is dit boek dat ik lees.
Wij zijn het die de fout gemaakt hebben.

tables.caption_tr: Negative and Interrogative Clefts
rows: Het is niet Jan die dat zei, maar Piet.
Wie is het die dat gezegd heeft?
Wat is het dat je zo boos maakt?

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Cleft Sentences
rows: Het is het boek die ik lees.
'boek' is a het-word and requires 'dat', not 'die'
Het is het boek dat ik lees.
Het is de kinderen die spelen.
Het zijn de kinderen die spelen.
Het was Jan die is gekomen.
Mixing past and present perfect across the two clauses sounds awkward; keep the tense parallel
footnotes_tr: In casual spoken Dutch, native speakers sometimes use 'die' even where 'dat' would be grammatically expected (e.g. after het-words); this is considered informal or substandard in written Dutch.

examples.target: Het is Jan die dat gezegd heeft.
examples.translation_tr: It is Jan who said that.
examples.note_tr: Focus on 'Jan' (a person) → die is used.

examples.target: Het is de auto die kapot is.
examples.translation_tr: It is the car that is broken.
examples.note_tr: 'de auto' is a de-word (common gender) → die.

examples.target: Het is het boek dat ik lees.
examples.translation_tr: It is the book that I am reading.
examples.note_tr: 'het boek' is a het-word (neuter) → dat.

examples.target: Het zijn de kinderen die buiten spelen.
examples.translation_tr: It is the children who are playing outside.
examples.note_tr: Plural focus → zijn (not is) + die.

examples.target: Het was Marie die kookte.
examples.translation_tr: It was Marie who was cooking.
examples.note_tr: Past tense: the copula 'was' matches the tense of the embedded clause.

examples.target: Het is niet Jan die dat zei, maar Piet.
examples.translation_tr: It is not Jan who said that, but Piet.
examples.note_tr: Negative cleft used to correct or contrast information.

examples.target: Wie is het die dat gezegd heeft?
examples.translation_tr: Who is it that said that?
examples.note_tr: Interrogative cleft asking about the focused person.

examples.target: Het is het beste wat je kunt doen.
examples.translation_tr: It is the best thing you can do.
examples.note_tr: 'wat' is used after a superlative used as a noun (het beste).

correlative-conjunctions.intro_tr: Correlative conjunctions are word-pairs that link two parallel elements; words, phrases, or clauses; into a single balanced statement, such as 'both...and' or 'neither...nor' in English. Dutch has a small but important set of these pairs (zowel...als, niet alleen...maar ook, of...of, hetzij...hetzij, noch...noch, enerzijds...anderzijds, deels...deels), several of which belong to a more formal, written register typical of C1-level and official texts. The trickiest part for learners is not the pairs themselves but two side-effects: (1) verb agreement when the two linked items are singular/plural or different persons, and (2) word order, since some pairs (niet alleen, noch) trigger inversion when they open the sentence, much like negative adverbs. This page gives the full set of pairs, their register, the agreement rules, and the inversion patterns so you can use them accurately in both speech and formal writing.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of Dutch correlative conjunction pairs
rows: Neutral to slightly formal; the most common and versatile pair, works with nouns, adjectives, and clauses.
Emphatic; triggers subject-verb inversion when it opens the sentence.
Neutral, everyday register; simplest way to present two alternatives.
Formal, written register; typical of legal, administrative, or academic texts.
A slightly less formal variant of hetzij...hetzij, still written register.
Formal; itself carries negation, so niet/geen must never be added separately.
on the one hand ... on the other hand
Discourse-level pair for contrasting two arguments or viewpoints.
Neutral to formal; distributes a quality or amount between two aspects.

tables.caption_tr: Word order effects of correlative conjunctions
rows: Zowel Anna als Tom komt vanavond.
zowel...als never triggers inversion, even at the start of the sentence; normal V2 order applies.
niet alleen ... maar (ook); inversion when clause-initial
Niet alleen is hij slim, maar hij is ook aardig.
Like negative adverbs (nauwelijks, zelden), niet alleen at the front of a clause forces subject-verb inversion (is hij, not hij is).
niet alleen ... maar ook; no inversion mid-sentence
Hij is niet alleen slim, maar ook aardig.
When niet alleen appears after the subject, normal word order is used; no inversion needed.
noch ... noch; normal order, negation absorbed
Noch Jan noch Piet komt vanavond.
noch...noch functions as the subject group; the finite verb still occupies second position, and no extra niet/geen is added.
Hetzij je komt, hetzij je belt af.
Each hetzij introduces a full parallel clause or option; word order within each clause is normal (main clause V2).
enerzijds ... anderzijds; adverbial, triggers inversion when first
Enerzijds begrijp ik het probleem, anderzijds zie ik geen oplossing.
As a fronted adverb, enerzijds triggers inversion (begrijp ik), just like any other sentence-initial adverb in V2 order.

tables.caption_tr: Verb agreement with correlative subject pairs
rows: Zowel de vader als de moeder werkt.
Verb is typically singular, agreeing with the idea of each subject separately, though plural is also accepted in informal use.
Zowel de leraar als de leerlingen waren tevreden.
Verb usually agrees with the nearest (last-mentioned) subject; here plural leerlingen gives waren.
Standard Dutch uses a singular verb, agreeing with the sense that each subject individually fails to act.
Of Jan of Piet komt langs.
Singular verb, treating the alternative as one single (unspecified) subject.
Hetzij de directeur hetzij zijn plaatsvervanger tekent het contract.
Singular verb, same logic as of...of; only one of the two will actually perform the action.
footnotes_tr: In spoken Dutch, plural verbs after these pairs are increasingly heard, but the singular remains the prescribed standard-language choice.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with correlative conjunctions
rows: zowel must always be paired with als, never with en.
Hetzij je komt, en hetzij je belt af.
Hetzij je komt, hetzij je belt af.
hetzij pairs with a second hetzij (or of), not with en.
Noch Jan noch Piet komt niet.
noch already expresses negation; adding niet creates an incorrect double negative.
Niet alleen hij is slim, maar hij is ook aardig.
Niet alleen is hij slim, maar hij is ook aardig.
When niet alleen opens the sentence, the subject and finite verb must invert.
Of...of gebruikt met drie opties zonder herhaling.
Of A, of B, of C (herhaal 'of' voor elke optie).
Each additional alternative in a list needs its own of/hetzij, not just a comma.

examples.target: Zowel mijn broer als mijn zus spreekt Frans.
examples.translation_tr: Both my brother and my sister speak French.
examples.note_tr: zowel...als links two subjects; the verb usually agrees with the nearer/last subject (singular here).

examples.target: Noch de directeur noch zijn assistent was aanwezig.
examples.translation_tr: Neither the director nor his assistant was present.
examples.note_tr: noch already means 'nor'; never add niet or geen alongside it.

examples.target: Je kunt hetzij per e-mail, hetzij telefonisch reageren.
examples.translation_tr: You can respond either by email or by phone.
examples.note_tr: hetzij...hetzij is formal/written register, common in official texts.

examples.target: Niet alleen was het duur, maar het smaakte ook niet.
examples.translation_tr: Not only was it expensive, but it also didn't taste good.
examples.note_tr: When niet alleen opens the sentence, subject-verb inversion is required (was het).

examples.target: Of we gaan nu, of we gaan helemaal niet.
examples.translation_tr: Either we go now, or we don't go at all.
examples.note_tr: of...of is the neutral, everyday alternative to hetzij...hetzij.

examples.target: Enerzijds wil ik verhuizen, anderzijds hou ik van mijn buurt.
examples.translation_tr: On the one hand I want to move, on the other hand I love my neighborhood.
examples.note_tr: A discourse-level correlative pair used to contrast two viewpoints.

examples.target: Het plan is deels goed doordacht, deels erg riskant.
examples.translation_tr: The plan is partly well thought out, partly very risky.
examples.note_tr: deels...deels distributes a quality between two aspects.

examples.target: Zowel de leraar als de leerlingen waren tevreden met het resultaat.
examples.translation_tr: Both the teacher and the students were satisfied with the result.
examples.note_tr: With mixed singular/plural subjects, the verb often takes the plural form.

formal-prepositional-phrases.title_tr: Formal Prepositional Phrases (ten aanzien van, met betrekking tot)
formal-prepositional-phrases.intro_tr: Formal prepositional phrases such as ten aanzien van and met betrekking tot are multi-word prepositions typical of written, official, legal, and academic Dutch. They replace simple prepositions like over, voor, or door with a more elevated, bureaucratic tone, and are extremely common in letters, reports, laws, and news articles, though rare in everyday speech. Many of these phrases still contain fossilized case forms (ten = archaic dative of te + den, ter = te + der), remnants of the old Dutch case system. Most are followed by a noun phrase introduced by 'van', and when placed at the start of a sentence they trigger normal V2 inversion just like any other fronted element. Recognizing and correctly using this register is essential for reading official documents and writing formally in Dutch (C1 level).

tables.caption_tr: Core Formal Prepositional Phrases
rows: in view of, with a view to
on the grounds of, based on
as part of, in the context of
chargeable to, at the cost of

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison by Meaning
rows: ten aanzien van / met betrekking tot
in verband met / op grond van

tables.caption_tr: Syntax: Position and Combination Patterns
rows: Fronting triggers V2 inversion, same as any other topicalized element
Neutral, unmarked position; common in formal reports
The article is normally required with the noun that follows
Turns a verb into a noun phrase, typical of bureaucratic style
ten aanzien hiervan / met betrekking hiertoe
'hier-' compounds replace 'van dit/deze' in very formal register

tables.caption_tr: Archaic Case Remnants Inside Formal Phrases
rows: fossilized in ten aanzien van, ten behoeve van, ten koste van
fossilized in ter attentie van, ter zake van, ter plaatse
old genitive/dative feminine or plural article
survives in fixed legal phrases like namens der regering (rare, very formal)
footnotes_tr: These forms are frozen relics; they are not productive in modern Dutch and cannot be used to form new phrases.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: Using 'ten aanzien van' in casual conversation
Wrong preposition; the fixed form uses 'met'
'van' is an obligatory part of the phrase
Using 'ten opzichte van' to mean 'because of'
It means 'relative to/compared to', not causation
Use 'op grond van' or 'vanwege' for cause
They are frozen archaic case forms, not the preposition 'te' + article
Learn each phrase as a fixed unit, do not decompose it

examples.target: Ten aanzien van de nieuwe wetgeving zijn nog veel vragen onbeantwoord.
examples.translation_tr: Regarding the new legislation, many questions remain unanswered.
examples.note_tr: 'ten aanzien van' fronted at the start of the sentence, triggering V2 inversion (verb 'zijn' comes before the subject 'veel vragen').

examples.target: Met betrekking tot uw verzoek kunnen wij u het volgende meedelen.
examples.translation_tr: With regard to your request, we can inform you of the following.
examples.note_tr: Typical opening of a formal letter or official reply.

examples.target: De maatregelen zijn genomen met het oog op de veiligheid van de bewoners.
examples.translation_tr: The measures were taken with a view to the residents' safety.
examples.note_tr: 'met het oog op' expresses purpose/goal, similar to 'in order to ensure'.

examples.target: Naar aanleiding van uw klacht hebben wij een onderzoek ingesteld.
examples.translation_tr: Following your complaint, we have initiated an investigation.
examples.note_tr: 'naar aanleiding van' is used to introduce the trigger/cause for an official action.

examples.target: In verband met de feestdagen is het kantoor gesloten.
examples.translation_tr: Due to the holidays, the office is closed.
examples.note_tr: 'in verband met' gives a reason, common on notices and signs.

examples.target: Deze subsidie wordt verstrekt ten behoeve van kleine ondernemingen.
examples.translation_tr: This subsidy is provided for the benefit of small businesses.
examples.note_tr: 'ten behoeve van' is a formal equivalent of 'voor'.

examples.target: Ondanks de kritiek heeft de minister het besluit gehandhaafd.
examples.translation_tr: Despite the criticism, the minister upheld the decision.
examples.note_tr: 'ondanks' is the neutral form; 'niettegenstaande' is the more formal/legal equivalent.

examples.target: Op grond van artikel 12 is de vergunning ingetrokken.
examples.translation_tr: On the basis of article 12, the permit has been revoked.
examples.note_tr: 'op grond van' introduces a legal or logical basis for a decision.

text-connectors.intro_tr: Text connectors (verbindingswoorden) are adverbs that link sentences or clauses to signal how ideas relate to each other: addition, contrast, cause/result, or conclusion. Unlike simple coordinating conjunctions such as en or maar, these words behave as full clause elements: when placed at the very start of a sentence they occupy position 1, pushing the finite verb into position 2 and forcing the subject to follow the verb (inversion). Many of them can also appear later in the clause, right after the subject, in which case no inversion occurs. This page groups the main connectors by logical function and flags register, since several of them (bijgevolg, derhalve, tevens) belong to formal or written Dutch while others (dus, toch, ook) are common in everyday speech.

tables.caption_tr: Addition connectors
rows: neutral-formal; adds a stronger, often decisive extra point
neutral; very common in both writing and speech
neutral; also used to introduce a new topic

tables.caption_tr: Contrast and concession connectors
rows: on the other hand / in contrast
contrasts two different subjects/entities; rarely opens a sentence with no prior contrastive context
never in first position; typically placed right after the subject or finite verb
refers back to a fact already mentioned
weaker and more conversational than desondanks/niettemin
similar to desondanks but slightly more formal/literary
stronger than daarentegen; flatly denies the previous statement

tables.caption_tr: Cause and result connectors
rows: as a result / because of that
refers to a cause already mentioned
very frequent; can be clause-initial or mid-clause
similar to dus but slightly more formal
typical of academic and legal texts

tables.caption_tr: Conclusion and summary connectors

word-formation.intro_tr: Dutch enriches its vocabulary through a small set of highly productive suffixes that shift one word class into another. -heid attaches to adjectives to build abstract de-nouns (vrij → vrijheid, "freedom"). -baar attaches to verb stems to build adjectives meaning "able to be ...-ed" (eten → eetbaar, "edible"). -lijk is the most versatile of the four: it derives adjectives from nouns, verbs, or other adjectives, often meaning "-ly", "-al", or expressing possibility (gevaar → gevaarlijk, "dangerous"; mogen → mogelijk, "possible"). -achtig attaches mainly to nouns and means "-ish" or "resembling" (kind → kinderachtig, "childish"). When these suffixes are added, watch for small but predictable spelling and stem changes (open-syllable vowel reduction, v/z-to-f/s devoicing, linking -e-), and remember that the negative prefix on- combines freely with most -baar and -lijk adjectives (mogelijk → onmogelijk, "impossible").

compound-nouns.intro_tr: Dutch compound nouns are written as a single word (unlike English, which often uses two separate words), and the two parts are sometimes joined directly, sometimes joined with a linking -s-, and sometimes joined with a linking -en-. There is no single logical rule that predicts the correct linking sound with 100% accuracy; the choice is historically rooted (old genitive -s vs. old plural -en) and many common words are simply exceptions that must be memorized or checked in a dictionary. As a rough guide, abstract nouns ending in -heid, -teit, -ing, -schap, -dom and agent nouns ending in -er/-aar tend to trigger -s-, while nouns denoting living beings or nouns whose plural is in -en tend to trigger -en-; but frequent, well-known exceptions exist (oogarts, dagboek, stadhuis). The gender (de/het) and the plural form of the whole compound are always determined by the LAST element (the head noun), and the main stress normally falls on the FIRST element of the compound.

punctuation-style.intro_tr: Dutch spelling has a handful of tricky, rule-governed details that are not intuitive for English speakers: the "tussen-n" (linking -n) that appears inside many compound nouns, the apostrophe used both for certain plurals and for possessives, the trema (diaeresis) that keeps neighboring vowels from merging into one sound, and the hyphen used instead of a trema at compound boundaries. Unlike English, these choices in Dutch are governed by fairly precise (if occasionally exception-ridden) rules tied to plural forms and vowel combinations, rather than by feel. This page collects the core rules, the main exception patterns (like kippensoep vs. kipfilet), and the everyday contracted forms ('t, 'n, 's, 'm, 'r) so you can check spelling and punctuation decisions at a glance. Mastering these details is largely a C1-level, "polish your writing" skill; native speakers themselves often have to double-check them.

archaic-case-remnants.title_tr: Fixed Expressions and Traces of the Old Case System (der, des, te allen tijde)
archaic-case-remnants.intro_tr: Modern standard Dutch abolished grammatical case (nominative/genitive/dative/accusative) on nouns and articles in the 20th century, and spoken Dutch today only distinguishes common (de) and neuter (het) gender. However, a layer of fixed, unproductive expressions; mostly formal, legal, or literary; still carries fossilized case endings from the old three-gender, four-case system. The two key fossils are "der" (old genitive/dative of "de") and "des" (old genitive of "de/het"), plus their fused-with-"te" forms "ter" and "ten". These forms cannot be generated freely: they exist only inside a closed list of set phrases that must be memorized as whole chunks, the same way an English learner memorizes "to and fro" without analyzing "fro" separately. As a beginner, your goal is simply to recognize these phrases when you meet them in formal writing, place names, and common time expressions; never to build new sentences with "der/des/ter/ten" on your own.

literary-tenses.title_tr: Literary Narrative Tenses and the Historical Present
literary-tenses.intro_tr: In Dutch literary and journalistic narration, tense choice often departs from everyday spoken conventions to create stylistic effect. The most striking device is the 'historical present' (historisch presens), where present-tense verbs narrate past events, lending immediacy and vividness. Literary prose also strongly prefers the simple past (imperfectum) over the perfectum for background narration, reserving the perfectum mainly for spoken registers or explicitly completed results. Writers frequently shift tenses mid-narrative; switching into the present at a dramatic peak, then back to the past; a technique found in novels, fairy tales, historical accounts, and sports or news reporting. Recognizing these shifts is essential for advanced reading comprehension, since no formal marker other than the verb form itself signals the change.

complex-passive-transforms.intro_tr: Dutch has two everyday passive voices built with worden (process) and zijn (resulting state), but there is a third, distinctly Dutch construction: the krijgen-passive. It is used when a sentence has both a direct object and an indirect object (a recipient), and that recipient; instead of the thing being transferred; becomes the grammatical subject. English has no exact equivalent; it usually just says "I got/was given X," which is precisely the nuance krijgen captures. This construction combines with all tenses, with modals, and with a large family of fixed "krijgen + te + infinitive" idioms (te horen krijgen, te zien krijgen, opgelegd krijgen). Because krijgen behaves like an auxiliary here (much like worden), it also follows the same verb-cluster word-order rules in perfect tenses, where two participles stack up at the end of the clause.

examples.target: De kinderen krijgen elke avond een verhaaltje voorgelezen.
examples.translation_tr: The children are read a story every evening.
examples.note_tr: Present tense krijgen-passive with a habitual action.

examples.target: Zou je liever een cadeaubon aangeboden krijgen?
examples.translation_tr: Would you rather be offered a gift card?
examples.note_tr: Conditional 'zou' combined with the krijgen-passive.

examples.target: Na het examen kregen de studenten hun cijfers direct te zien.
examples.translation_tr: After the exam, the students got to see their grades immediately.
examples.note_tr: Fixed expression 'te zien krijgen' = to get to see.

examples.target: Hij kreeg een boete opgelegd omdat hij te hard reed.
examples.translation_tr: He was fined because he was driving too fast.
examples.note_tr: 'opgelegd krijgen' = to have (a fine, rule, etc.) imposed on you.

ellipsis-gapping.title_tr: Ellipsis and Gapping (Leaving Out Repeated Words)
ellipsis-gapping.intro_tr: Dutch, just like English, avoids repeating words that the listener can already predict from context. This general strategy is called ellipsis (weglating), and one common type of it; deleting a repeated verb in a coordinated sentence; is specifically called gapping. You will meet this in four everyday situations: dropping a repeated verb after 'en/maar/of', dropping a repeated infinitive after modal verbs, dropping a noun after an adjective (die grote, de kleine), and giving short answers instead of full sentences. Even though this is treated as an advanced topic, the underlying logic is simple: never repeat information the other person already has. Learning the patterns below will make your Dutch sound much more natural and less "textbook."

tables.caption_tr: Overview: The main types of ellipsis in Dutch
rows: the finite verb (sometimes more) in a later coordinated clause
Jan eet vis en Piet [eet] vlees.
a repeated infinitive after a modal/auxiliary
Ik kan het niet, maar hij kan het wel [doen].
'gaan/komen' after a modal, when a destination is given
a noun already mentioned, after an adjective
Neem de rode [appel], niet de groene [appel].
the whole predicate, in a short answer
Ga je mee? – Ja, ik ga [mee].
Zij werkt harder dan hij [werkt hard].
an entire clause except one contrastive word

tables.caption_tr: Gapping in coordinated clauses: the rules
rows: Only the finite verb (and anything after it that is identical) is deleted
Jan koopt een auto en Piet [koopt] een fiets.
'koopt' is repeated and identical in both clauses, so it is dropped in the second.
Gapping only works in coordination, never in subordinate clauses
Jan eet vis en Piet vlees. (correct) / *omdat Jan vis eet en Piet vlees (impossible without repeating 'eet')
Subordinators (omdat, dat, als...) block gapping; the verb must stay.
The verb form must be truly identical (same tense, same person agreement is not required, but same lexical verb is)
Ik las een boek en zij een krant.
Both 'las' clauses use the same past-tense verb 'las', so it can be gapped.
The surviving constituents keep contrastive stress and normal word order
Jan drinkt WIJN en Piet BIER.
The remaining nouns carry the emphasis since the verb is gone.
A separable verb's particle can also be gapped along with the finite verb
Hij belt zijn moeder op en zij haar vader [belt ... op].
Both the finite verb and the separable particle disappear together.
Gapping normally cannot leave just a bare subject with nothing else new
*Jan werkt en Piet. (unnatural without an added constituent)
There must be at least one new, contrasting element left in the second clause.

tables.caption_tr: Nominal ellipsis (N-ellipsis): dropping the noun after an adjective
rows: Ik wil de grote, niet de kleine.
een grote (adds -e once the noun is dropped!)
Ik zoek geen klein huis, ik zoek een grote.
Dit is het mooiste dat ik heb.

tables.caption_tr: Answer and fragment ellipsis in conversation
rows: Ga je morgen mee naar het feest?
Ja, ik ga morgen mee naar het feest.
Ja, ik ga mee. / Ja, ik ga.
Heb je het boek al gelezen?
Nee, ik heb het boek nog niet gelezen.
Ik kom niet omdat ik ziek ben.

tables.caption_tr: Restrictions: what cannot be omitted
rows: Different verb forms in the two clauses
Gapping requires the exact same verb form; if tense or verb differs, it must stay
*Jan werkte en Piet werkt gisteren. → Jan werkte gisteren en Piet werkt vandaag.
The finite verb in a subordinate clause cannot be gapped away
*...omdat Jan koffie en Piet thee → ...omdat Jan koffie drinkt en Piet thee drinkt.
The very first clause of a coordination
Ellipsis always targets the second (or later) clause, never the first
*[eet] vis en Jan vlees → Jan eet vis en Piet [eet] vlees.
Adjective ending after noun-drop with het-words
When the noun is dropped, an otherwise uninflected adjective before a het-word must take -e
If dropping the word would create confusion about who does what, Dutch keeps the verb explicit
Jan helpt Piet en Klaas helpt Marie. (not gapped, to avoid ambiguity about who helps whom)

examples.target: Jan drinkt koffie en Marie thee.
examples.translation_tr: Jan drinks coffee and Marie [drinks] tea.
examples.note_tr: Gapping: the verb 'drinkt' is dropped in the second clause because it is identical.

examples.target: Ik wil niet, maar ik moet wel.
examples.translation_tr: I don't want to, but I have to [do it].
examples.note_tr: Verb cluster ellipsis: 'het doen' is understood and left out; 'wel' carries the contrast.

examples.target: Neem de grote, niet de kleine.
examples.translation_tr: Take the big one, not the small one.
examples.note_tr: N-ellipsis: the noun (e.g. 'appel') is dropped after the adjective, which keeps its -e ending.

examples.target: Ga je morgen mee? – Ja, ik ga.
examples.translation_tr: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Yes, I am [going].
examples.note_tr: Short answer keeps subject+verb but drops the repeated adverb 'mee'.

examples.target: Ik moet naar de dokter.
examples.translation_tr: I have to [go] to the doctor.
examples.note_tr: Directional ellipsis: the infinitive 'gaan' after the modal 'moet' is omitted because the destination makes it obvious.

examples.target: Zij is slimmer dan hij.
examples.translation_tr: She is smarter than he [is].
examples.note_tr: Comparative ellipsis: 'is' after 'hij' is left out in the 'dan'-clause.

examples.target: Jan komt vanavond, Piet niet.
examples.translation_tr: Jan is coming tonight, Piet isn't.
examples.note_tr: Stripping: the whole predicate is reduced to just the polarity word 'niet'.

examples.target: Wil je thee of koffie? – Koffie, graag.
examples.translation_tr: Do you want tea or coffee? – Coffee, please.
examples.note_tr: Fragment answer: only the requested item is named, the rest of the sentence is omitted.

nested-subclauses.title_tr: Nested Subordinate Clauses and Long-Distance Dependencies
nested-subclauses.intro_tr: Dutch subordinate clauses always push their finite verb (and any accompanying verbs) to the very end of the clause; but when clauses are embedded inside other clauses, this rule applies again and again, one layer at a time. Each new 'dat', 'die', or 'of' clause creates its own separate verb-final slot, so deeply nested sentences end up with several verbs scattered across several clause boundaries rather than one giant pile. To keep long sentences readable, Dutch often extraposes heavy clauses (especially relative clauses and clausal complements) to the very end of the sentence, creating a long-distance link between a noun near the front and its clause far at the back. Relative pronouns can also 'reach into' an embedded clause across so-called bridge verbs like denken, zeggen, or geloven, producing long-distance dependencies. Finally, when a modal or perception verb is itself embedded inside a perfect-tense verb cluster, it surfaces as an infinitive instead of a participle; the IPP effect; which is a frequent source of errors in nested constructions.

tables.caption_tr: Stacking dat-clauses: each level of embedding adds its own verb-final position
rows: He says that he is coming.
Ik denk dat hij zegt dat hij komt.
2 nested clauses: [dat hij zegt [dat hij komt]]
I think that he says that he is coming.
Ik hoop dat je weet dat ik denk dat het waar is.
3 nested clauses, each with its own verb at the end
I hope that you know that I think it's true.
footnotes_tr: Each subordinate verb (zegt, weet, denk, is) stays at the end of its OWN clause; the verbs from different embedding levels never merge into a single cluster, because every 'dat' opens a fresh clause boundary.

tables.caption_tr: Extraposition: heavy relative/complement clauses move to the very end to avoid center-embedding
rows: Een vrouw die ik nog nooit had ontmoet, belde op.
Er belde een vrouw op die ik nog nooit had ontmoet.
A woman I had never met called.
Een man die, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam, groette ons.
Een man groette ons die, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam.
A man who, although ill, still came, greeted us.
Het feit dat hij loog verbaasde niemand.
Niemand was verbaasd, want het was bekend dat hij loog.
Nobody was surprised, since it was known that he lied.
footnotes_tr: Extraposition creates a long-distance dependency: the antecedent ('een vrouw', 'een man') and its relative clause are no longer adjacent, but Dutch speakers reliably reconnect them across the intervening verb.
This strategy is strongly preferred whenever the relative/complement clause is long, keeping the subject-verb link short and the sentence easy to parse.

tables.caption_tr: Long-distance relative clauses across bridge verbs (denken, zeggen, geloven, beweren, horen, hopen)
rows: het boek dat ik denk dat hij gelezen heeft
the book that I think he has read
'dat' is the object of 'gelezen heeft' two clauses down, not of 'denk'
de vrouw die ze zeggen dat verhuisd is
the woman who they say has moved
de plek waar hij beweerde dat hij geboren was
the place where he claimed he was born
'waar' relativizes an element inside the embedded clause
footnotes_tr: This long-distance extraction works smoothly with reportative/'bridge' verbs (denken, zeggen, geloven, beweren, horen, hopen) that introduce open, assertable complement clauses.
It becomes much harder or impossible with factive/emotive verbs such as betreuren (to regret) or verbs that do not easily embed a plain dat-clause.

tables.caption_tr: The IPP effect (Infinitivus Pro Participio) in nested verb clusters
rows: He has done it. / He has had to do it.
Ik heb hem zien vertrekken. (not 'gezien vertrekken')
I saw him. / I saw him leave.
Zij heeft het boek willen lezen. (not 'gewild lezen')
She has read the book. / She has wanted to read the book.
footnotes_tr: IPP replaces the expected past participle of modal, causative, and perception verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, laten, zien, horen, helpen) with their infinitive form whenever they head a verb cluster together with another infinitive under 'hebben'.
This effect is easy to forget precisely because it only shows up once a second verb is embedded; i.e., in nested constructions.

tables.caption_tr: Frequent mistakes when clauses are embedded several levels deep
rows: Merging verb-final positions across clause levels
Ik denk dat hij komt zegt.
Ik denk dat hij zegt dat hij komt.
Each dat-clause needs its own complementizer and its own verb-final slot; verbs from different embedding levels cannot be merged into one cluster.
A modal verb embedded under a perfect auxiliary surfaces as an infinitive, not a participle.
Een man die, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam, groette ons.
Een man groette ons die, hoewel hij ziek was, toch kwam.
Extraposing the relative clause to the end avoids an unreadable 'sandwich' structure around the main verb.
Ik weet niet dat of hij komt.
Ik weet niet of hij komt.
Only one complementizer per clause is allowed; 'of' already marks the embedded question, so 'dat' is not added.

examples.target: Ik denk dat hij zegt dat hij het niet meer weet.
examples.translation_tr: I think that he says that he doesn't know anymore.
examples.note_tr: Two stacked dat-clauses: each has its own verb-final position (zegt, weet).

examples.target: Er kwam een man binnen die niemand kende.
examples.translation_tr: A man whom nobody knew came in.
examples.note_tr: The relative clause is extraposed to the end instead of sitting right after 'een man', avoiding a heavy subject.

examples.target: Het boek dat ik denk dat hij gelezen heeft, ligt op tafel.
examples.translation_tr: The book that I think he has read is lying on the table.
examples.note_tr: Long-distance relativization: 'dat' is understood as the object of 'gelezen heeft', two clauses down, across the bridge verb 'denk'.

examples.target: Hij heeft het helaas niet meer kunnen navertellen.
examples.translation_tr: Unfortunately, he was no longer able to retell it.
examples.note_tr: IPP effect: 'kunnen' stays an infinitive (not 'gekund') because it heads a verb cluster with another infinitive under 'heeft'.

examples.target: Ik hoop dat je weet dat ik denk dat het waar is.
examples.translation_tr: I hope that you know that I think it's true.
examples.note_tr: Three levels of embedding; every dat-clause keeps its own finite verb at its own clause boundary.

examples.target: De vrouw die ze zeggen dat verhuisd is, was mijn buurvrouw.
examples.translation_tr: The woman who they say has moved was my neighbor.
examples.note_tr: Long-distance subject relativization across the bridge verb 'zeggen dat'.

examples.target: Een man groette ons die, hoewel hij ziek was, toch gekomen was.
examples.translation_tr: A man who, although he was ill, had still come, greeted us.
examples.note_tr: Extraposing the relative clause after the main verb keeps the sentence readable instead of center-embedding it between subject and verb.

stylistic-inversion.title_tr: Stylistic Inversion and Heavy Constituent Shift
stylistic-inversion.intro_tr: Beyond the obligatory Verb-Second (V2) rule, Dutch allows subject-verb order to be manipulated for rhetorical and stylistic effect; this is called stylistic inversion. It appears after direct quotations, fronted negative/emphatic adverbs, literary narrative markers like 'aldus', and in formal conditional clauses where 'als' is dropped and the verb moves to first position instead. A related but distinct phenomenon is heavy constituent shift (extraposition): long or complex elements such as relative clauses, comparative clauses, and heavy prepositional phrases are moved out of the crowded 'middle field' and placed after the verb cluster, in the sentence-final 'nafield', to keep sentences readable. Placeholder words like 'het' and 'er' are often used to hold the front position while the real (heavy) subject or clause is pushed to the end. These patterns belong mainly to formal written and literary registers and are rarely used in casual speech.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Stylistic Inversion
rows: Fronted negative or restrictive adverb (nooit, zelden, nauwelijks)
Emphatic; the inversion itself is regular V2, but choosing to front the adverb is a stylistic choice
Standard in narrative and dialogue writing; the quote occupies the front position, forcing V-S order in the tag
Was ik rijk, dan reisde ik de wereld rond.
Formal/literary; the finite verb replaces 'als' at the start of the conditional clause
High literary register, typical of storytelling and formal prose
Descriptive/narrative opening, common in fairy tales and literary description
Onder de brug woonde een oude visser.
Fairy-tale/narrative style, gives dramatic emphasis to the setting

tables.caption_tr: Heavy Constituent Shift (Extraposition) Rules
rows: Ik heb het boek gelezen dat iedereen aanraadt.
Hij is groter geworden dan ik had verwacht.
Ze heeft gesproken met alle mensen die op de vergadering aanwezig waren.
Hij heeft besloten te vertrekken naar een stad waar niemand hem kent.
Replaced by 'het' at front, clause moved to the end
Het is duidelijk dat hij gelijk heeft.
'Er' + verb ..., heavy subject moved to the end
Er liepen drie mannen het plein op die niemand kende.

tables.caption_tr: Placeholder Elements Used in Heavy Shift
rows: Dummy subject standing in for a postponed clausal subject
Het verbaasde iedereen dat hij zo laat kwam.
Existential/presentational placeholder for a postponed heavy indefinite subject
Er is een man aan de deur die je wil spreken.
Direct extraposition of a relative or comparative clause without any dummy element
Ik ken de vrouw niet die daar woont.

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Comparison: Neutral vs Stylistically Shifted
rows: Quotative inversion after fronted direct speech
Ik heb nog nooit zoiets moois gezien.
Nog nooit heb ik zoiets moois gezien.
Fronting the negative adverb for emphasis
Als ik tijd had, zou ik komen.
Had ik tijd, dan zou ik komen.
Ik heb het boek dat je aanraadde gelezen.
Ik heb het boek gelezen dat je aanraadde.
Heavy relative clause extraposed to the end for a more balanced, readable sentence

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes
rows: Redundantly combines 'als' with verb-first conditional inversion; only one strategy should be used
Was ik rijk, dan... (drop 'als' when inverting)
Always leaving heavy relative clauses in the middle field
Grammatically possible but sounds clumsy and hard to process in written Dutch
Ik heb het boek gelezen dat iedereen aanraadt. (shift the clause to the end)
Violates V2: the quote occupies the front position, so the verb must come before the subject
Overusing literary inversion patterns (Aldus, Was ik...) in casual speech
These patterns belong to formal written/literary register and sound unnatural or archaic in everyday conversation
Use 'als' + straight word order in speech: Als ik rijk was, dan...

examples.target: Nooit had ik zoiets verwacht.
examples.translation_tr: I had never expected such a thing.
examples.note_tr: Fronting the negative adverb 'nooit' (never) triggers inversion of subject and verb; this is used for rhetorical emphasis in formal/literary Dutch.

examples.target: 'Ik ga nu weg,' zei ze boos.
examples.translation_tr: 'I'm leaving now,' she said angrily.
examples.note_tr: After a direct quotation, the quote counts as the fronted element, so the verb-subject order 'zei ze' (not 'ze zei') is required; quotative inversion.

examples.target: Was ik jonger, dan zou ik met je meegaan.
examples.translation_tr: If I were younger, I would go with you.
examples.note_tr: Formal/literary conditional inversion: the conjunction 'als' is dropped and the finite verb moves to the front of the clause instead; 'dan' often introduces the main clause.

examples.target: Aldus eindigde het verhaal van de oude visser.
examples.translation_tr: Thus ended the story of the old fisherman.
examples.note_tr: High literary/narrative marker 'aldus' (thus) obligatorily triggers subject-verb inversion; typical of storytelling or formal written prose.

examples.target: Ik heb de brief gelezen die al drie weken op mijn bureau lag.
examples.translation_tr: I read the letter that had been lying on my desk for three weeks.
examples.note_tr: The heavy relative clause 'die al drie weken op mijn bureau lag' is shifted past the verb cluster ('heb ... gelezen') into the sentence-final 'nafield' instead of sitting in the crowded middle field.

examples.target: Er kwam een man het café binnen die iedereen meteen herkende.
examples.translation_tr: A man whom everyone immediately recognized came into the café.
examples.note_tr: 'Er' acts as a placeholder subject so that the heavy indefinite subject 'een man ... die iedereen meteen herkende' can be shifted to the end of the sentence.

examples.target: Het is opmerkelijk dat niemand dit eerder heeft opgemerkt.
examples.translation_tr: It is remarkable that nobody has noticed this before.
examples.note_tr: 'Het' is a dummy subject standing in for the real clausal subject 'dat niemand dit eerder heeft opgemerkt', which is extraposed to the end.

dummy-subjects-advanced.intro_tr: Dutch cannot leave the first slot of a main clause empty, because the finite verb must always occupy the second position (the V2 rule). When there is no natural subject to place there; with weather verbs, impersonal passives, or clauses whose 'real' subject is a postponed dat-clause; Dutch inserts a semantically empty placeholder: 'het' or 'er'. At the advanced level, the challenge is not recognizing these dummy subjects but knowing precisely which one to use, when a second, different 'er' (existential, locative, quantitative, or prepositional) is required in the same sentence, and; crucially; when the dummy element must be deleted because another constituent has taken over the first position. This page maps out all of these advanced interactions systematically.

tables.caption_tr: The Four Functions of 'er' in Dutch
rows: Introduces an indefinite subject in 'there is/are' sentences
Er staat een fiets in de gang. / Er zijn veel problemen.
Obligatory whenever an indefinite subject would otherwise leave position 1 empty
Fills the subject slot when the logical subject is postponed and no other adverbial is fronted
Er loopt een hond op straat te blaffen.
Often co-occurs with existential 'er'; disappears once a locative phrase is fronted
Refers back to a noun already introduced, standing in for the omitted noun before a number or quantifier
Ik heb er drie gekocht. (I bought three of them)
Obligatory immediately before the numeral/quantifier when the noun itself is left out
Combines with a preposition to refer to a non-human antecedent instead of 'preposition + het/dat'
Ik denk er niet aan. (I'm not thinking about it)
Splits across the clause: 'er ... aan/op/mee' etc.; never 'aan het' for things

tables.caption_tr: 'het' as Dummy/Expletive Subject
rows: Het regent al de hele dag.
'het' is fully empty here and can never be replaced or omitted
Het is jammer dat je niet kunt komen.
The real subject is the postponed clause; 'het' merely holds position 1
Het werd besloten dat de vergadering doorging.
Alternates with 'Er werd besloten dat...'; 'het' sounds more formal/bureaucratic
'het' referring back to an entire preceding situation
Het regent, dat wist ik al.
Contrast with 'dat', which refers to the whole clause rather than repeating 'het'
Het is Jan die het gedaan heeft.
See the separate cleft-sentence topic for the full pattern

tables.caption_tr: Deletion and Retention Rules under Topicalization
rows: 'er' is dropped once a locative PP occupies position 1
Er staat een man in de tuin. → In de tuin staat een man.
'er' disappears if the indefinite subject itself is fronted (marked, contrastive use only)
Een man staat (er) in de tuin; normally avoided; 'er' construction preferred
'het' is retained and simply inverts with the verb; never dropped
'het' is omitted once the dat-clause itself is moved to position 1
Het is jammer dat hij ziek is. → Dat hij ziek is, is jammer.
'er' stays adjacent to the verb even when the numeral is fronted for emphasis

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Errors (Contrastive)
rows: *In de tuin staat er een man.
In de tuin staat een man.
Existential 'er' must be dropped once a locative phrase already fills position 1
Quantitative 'er' must precede the numeral/quantifier, not follow it
Er wordt gedanst. / Het wordt gedanst.
Only one dummy subject is allowed per clause; 'het' and 'er' can never combine in the same impersonal passive
*Er is jammer dat hij ziek is.
Het is jammer dat hij ziek is.
Extraposition of a clausal subject always requires 'het', never 'er'
A preposition referring to a non-human antecedent must fuse with 'er' (pronominal adverb), not combine with 'het'

tables.caption_tr: Quick Decision Table: 'het' or 'er'?
rows: Weather, time, or fully impersonal verbs
Yes; Het regent. / Het is laat.
Existential 'there is/are' with an indefinite subject
Extraposition of a clausal subject (dat-/om te-clause)
Impersonal passive with no logical subject
Yes (formal register); Het wordt gezegd dat...
Yes (neutral register); Er wordt gezegd dat... (never both together)
Referring back to an inanimate noun after a preposition
Yes; er + preposition (pronominal adverb), e.g. erover, ermee
Quantified or partitive reference ('some/three of them')
Yes; Ik heb er drie / er veel.

examples.target: Er wordt in dit dorp hard gewerkt.
examples.translation_tr: People work hard in this village. (impersonal passive using existential/impersonal 'er'; there is no real subject)

examples.target: Het is opvallend dat niemand iets zei.
examples.translation_tr: It is striking that nobody said anything. (extraposition: 'het' stands in for the postponed dat-clause, the real subject)

examples.target: In de kast liggen nog drie boeken.
examples.translation_tr: There are still three books in the cupboard. (the locative phrase 'in de kast' occupies position 1, so existential 'er' is dropped)

examples.target: Ik heb er nog twee over.
examples.translation_tr: I have two of them left. (quantitative 'er' refers back to an already-mentioned noun that is counted)

examples.target: Denkt hij er wel eens aan?
examples.translation_tr: Does he ever think about it? (prepositional 'er', split from 'aan', referring to a non-human antecedent)

examples.target: Het werd al snel duidelijk dat het plan mislukt was.
examples.translation_tr: It quickly became clear that the plan had failed. ('het' as extraposition subject with a passive-like copular construction)

examples.target: Er staat een oude eik midden op het plein.
examples.translation_tr: There is an old oak tree in the middle of the square. (classic existential 'er' introducing an indefinite subject)

examples.target: Dat hij zoiets zou doen, had niemand verwacht.
examples.translation_tr: Nobody had expected that he would do such a thing. (the dat-clause itself is fronted to position 1, so dummy 'het' is omitted entirely)

nominal-style.intro_tr: Nominal style (ambtelijk taalgebruik) is the formal, bureaucratic register used in Dutch official letters, laws, reports, and administrative forms. Its hallmark is nominalization: turning verbs into abstract nouns (behandelen → de behandeling) so that the noun, not the verb, carries the main information and becomes the grammatical subject or object. This style also favors passive and impersonal constructions (wordt, er wordt, men), long chains of prepositional phrases (met betrekking tot, ten aanzien van), and fixed formal vocabulary that replaces everyday words. The result is a dense, impersonal, and highly compressed text type that native speakers immediately recognize as "government language"; precise and neutral, but often criticized for being hard to read. Mastering it is essential for C2 learners who need to read or write official Dutch correspondence, legal texts, or policy documents.

tables.caption_tr: Nominalization: turning verbs into abstract nouns
The 'het + infinitive' pattern used as an abstract noun
rows: used as an abstract subject: 'the reading of the decision'

tables.caption_tr: Fixed formal prepositional phrases typical of official Dutch
Light-verb constructions: noun + support verb instead of a plain verb
Impersonal and passive markers that support the nominal style
rows: hides or omits the agent performing the action
Er wordt verzocht om tijdige aanlevering.
no grammatical subject at all; fully impersonal request
Men dient het formulier in te vullen.
Vaststelling van de datum geschiedt door de commissie.
an action noun, not a verb, is the grammatical subject

tables.caption_tr: Everyday vocabulary vs. formal/official vocabulary
Stacked noun phrases (chained van-constructions) typical of dense official prose
rows: de vaststelling van de hoogte van het bedrag
de indiening van het verzoek tot wijziging van de vergunning
het verzoek indienen om de vergunning te wijzigen
the filing of the request to amend the permit
de beoordeling van de gevolgen van het besluit
beoordelen wat de gevolgen van het besluit zijn
the assessment of the consequences of the decision

examples.target: De aanvraag tot vergunning wordt na ontvangst in behandeling genomen.
examples.translation_tr: The application for a permit will be processed upon receipt.
examples.note_tr: Passive construction (wordt genomen) plus nominalized 'aanvraag' and 'behandeling'; typical of official style.

examples.target: Ten aanzien van de gestelde vragen wordt het volgende opgemerkt.
examples.translation_tr: With respect to the questions raised, the following is noted.
examples.note_tr: Formal prepositional phrase 'ten aanzien van' plus impersonal passive 'wordt opgemerkt'.

examples.target: Men dient het formulier vóór 1 augustus in te dienen.
examples.translation_tr: The form must be submitted before August 1st.
examples.note_tr: Literally 'One must submit the form...'; 'men' avoids addressing the reader directly.

examples.target: De vaststelling van de nieuwe regeling geschiedt door het bestuur.
examples.translation_tr: The establishment of the new regulation is carried out by the board.
examples.note_tr: The noun 'vaststelling' (from vaststellen) functions as the grammatical subject instead of a verb.

examples.target: Naar aanleiding van uw schrijven delen wij u het volgende mede.
examples.translation_tr: In response to your letter, we hereby inform you of the following.
examples.note_tr: 'schrijven' used as a noun ('a letter/written communication'); 'mededelen' is the formal register of 'zeggen'.

examples.target: Er wordt verzocht om tijdige aanlevering van de benodigde documenten.
examples.translation_tr: You are kindly requested to submit the required documents in a timely manner.
examples.note_tr: Impersonal 'er wordt verzocht' plus nominalization 'aanlevering' instead of the verb 'aanleveren'.

examples.target: Het besluit tot afwijzing van de aanvraag is genomen op grond van artikel 5.
examples.translation_tr: The decision to reject the application was made on the basis of Article 5.
examples.note_tr: Chain of nominalizations: 'besluit', 'afwijzing', 'aanvraag', linked by 'tot' and 'van'; 'op grond van' is a fixed formal phrase.

examples.target: Onderhavig rapport bevat een overzicht van de bevindingen met betrekking tot het onderzoek.
examples.translation_tr: This report contains an overview of the findings with regard to the investigation.
examples.note_tr: 'onderhavig' ('the present/at hand') and 'met betrekking tot' are classic markers of bureaucratic register.

flemish-differences.title_tr: Belgian Flemish Differences (gij, ge, and word choice)
flemish-differences.intro_tr: Belgian Dutch (often called "Vlaams" or, in its everyday spoken form, "Tussentaal") shares the same standard written grammar (AN) as the Netherlands, but informal Belgian speech and casual writing show clear regional features. The most famous is the survival of the old pronoun pair gij/ge as an informal "you," alongside u used as both the polite pronoun and the informal object/possessive form; a system that disappeared from Netherlands Dutch centuries ago. Beyond pronouns, Belgian Dutch prefers many different everyday words (often French-influenced or archaic terms), has its own diminutive flavor, and uses different discourse habits and exclamations. These features are almost entirely restricted to spoken and informal registers; formal Belgian writing looks the same as Netherlands Dutch. This page collects the core gij/ge conjugation, pronoun forms, and the most common vocabulary substitutions you'll encounter in Flemish speech, dialogue, or informal text.

tables.caption_tr: Pronoun System: Standard Dutch vs. Belgian Flemish (gij/ge)
rows: GIJ moet dat doen. (YOU must do that.)
Ge moet dat doen. (You must do that.)
Ik zie u morgen. (I'll see you tomorrow.)
Is dat uw fiets? (Is that your bike?)
Wast ge u? (Are you washing yourself?)
Komt gij allemaal mee? (Are you all coming along?)
footnotes_tr: Gij/ge belongs to informal spoken registers and Tussentaal; formal written Belgian Dutch (AN) uses jij/u exactly like Netherlands Dutch.
Note that u in Belgian informal speech does double duty: it is both the polite pronoun (as in NL) and the informal object/possessive companion of gij; context and tone distinguish them.

tables.caption_tr: Verb Conjugation with gij (Present Tense & Imperative)
rows: 'zijt' is the classic marker of gij-conjugation, unique to this pronoun
same verb form, only the pronoun changes
regular -t ending is unchanged with gij
adding 'gij' after the imperative softens or emphasizes a command
in fast speech 'ge' often cliticizes onto the verb ending, e.g. 'werkte gij' → 'werkte-gij'

tables.caption_tr: Vocabulary Choices: Belgian Flemish vs. Netherlands Dutch
rows: what did you say? (asking to repeat)
beautiful, nice; a false friend! In NL Dutch 'schoon' means 'clean'
footnotes_tr: Many Belgian words are older Dutch forms or French loans (camion, chauffage, facteur) that were replaced by different words in the Netherlands over time.
'schoon' is the single most notorious false friend between the two varieties; always check context.

tables.caption_tr: Other Distinctive Grammatical and Stylistic Features
rows: Da's straf, hé! (That's crazy, isn't it!)
De facteur komt. vs. De postbode komt. (The mailman is coming.)
gij/ge in informal writing (chat, dialogue, subtitles)
virtually never used, feels archaic or biblical
Komde gij morgen? (informal Flemish chat) vs. Kom je morgen? (NL)
footnotes_tr: In the Netherlands, gij/ge survives only in Bible translations, old literature, and some southern (Brabantic/Limburgish) dialects, which is why it can sound old-fashioned to Dutch listeners even though it's completely everyday in Flanders.

examples.target: Gij zijt de max!
examples.translation_tr: You're the best! (typical Flemish use of gij as emphatic subject pronoun)

examples.target: Wat doet gij hier zo vroeg?
examples.translation_tr: What are you doing here so early? (gij instead of Standard Dutch jij)

examples.target: Woont gij nog bij uw ouders?
examples.translation_tr: Do you still live with your parents? (gij as subject, uw as possessive)

examples.target: Ik heb goesting in een ijsje.
examples.translation_tr: I feel like having an ice cream. (Belgian goesting vs Netherlands zin)

examples.target: Zet de fles in de frigo.
examples.translation_tr: Put the bottle in the fridge. (Belgian frigo vs Netherlands koelkast)

examples.target: Hij komt seffens terug.
examples.translation_tr: He'll be back in a moment. (Belgian seffens vs Netherlands straks)

examples.target: Amai, wat een gedoe zeg!
examples.translation_tr: Wow, what a hassle! (amai is a typical Flemish exclamation)

examples.target: Ik ga naar mijn kot in Leuven.
examples.translation_tr: I'm going to my student room in Leuven. (Belgian kot vs Netherlands studentenkamer)

idiomatic-structures.intro_tr: Dutch, like English, is full of frozen idiomatic expressions (vaste uitdrukkingen) and proverbs (spreekwoorden) whose meaning cannot be derived by translating the individual words. These chunks behave like single grammatical units: their word order, article choice, preposition, and even noun number are locked in place and often resist the normal flexibility of Dutch syntax (no passivization, no pluralizing, no swapping the fixed preposition). Some idioms also preserve archaic case endings (e.g., old dative forms) that survive only inside these fixed phrases. Because C2 mastery means recognizing and correctly reproducing these chunks rather than building them from grammar rules, the best strategy is to memorize each idiom as a whole unit, including its exact article, preposition, and word order. This page collects the most common structural patterns, together with example idioms and proverbs, so you can check both the meaning and the frozen grammar of each expression.

tables.caption_tr: Structural patterns that make idioms 'frozen' in grammar
rows: The article stays fixed as part of the chunk, even though article choice is normally tied to noun gender/definiteness
The preposition 'van' is locked to 'spijt' in this idiom; it cannot be replaced by another preposition
te allen tijde, ten koste van
These keep an old dative-style '-en' ending that is no longer productive anywhere else in modern Dutch
The verb and its object cannot usually be freely reordered, fronted, or passivized without breaking the idiomatic reading
The noun stays singular/definite exactly as fixed; you cannot pluralize or add extra modifiers freely
The separable verb still follows normal V2 / verb-second placement rules, but the combined meaning is non-compositional

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes with idioms and proverbs
rows: de kat de boom uit kijken

The fixed word order of the idiom must be preserved exactly; components cannot be reordered
The noun stays singular inside the fixed expression, even if logically 'knees' (plural) might seem to make sense
The archaic dative singular form 'tijde' is fixed; it is never pluralized to 'tijden' inside this expression
The article 'de' is an obligatory part of the fixed chunk and cannot be omitted
Look up the equivalent Dutch idiom instead
Idioms rarely translate literally between languages; always learn the whole Dutch chunk, not a word-by-word translation

examples.target: Laten we de kat uit de boom kijken voordat we iets beslissen.
examples.translation_tr: Let's wait and see (lit. 'watch the cat out of the tree') before we decide anything.
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiom meaning 'to hold back and observe the situation first'; word order is frozen and cannot be rearranged.

examples.target: Hij heeft het typen inmiddels goed onder de knie.
examples.translation_tr: He has meanwhile mastered typing well (lit. 'has it well under the knee').
examples.note_tr: 'iets onder de knie hebben' = to have mastered something; the noun 'knie' stays singular, never pluralized.

examples.target: We kwamen te laat en vonden de hond in de pot.
examples.translation_tr: We arrived too late and found the dog in the pot (i.e., all the food was already gone).
examples.note_tr: Classic proverb-like idiom for arriving after everything has been used up/eaten.

examples.target: Als de kat van huis is, dansen de muizen.
examples.translation_tr: When the cat's away, the mice will play.
examples.note_tr: Full proverb; note the inversion 'dansen de muizen' after the fronted 'als'-clause, following normal V2 rules.

examples.target: Hij zag door de bomen het bos niet meer.
examples.translation_tr: He could no longer see the forest for the trees (he lost the overview amid too many details).
examples.note_tr: The negation 'niet meer' and fixed noun phrase 'het bos' cannot be altered without breaking the idiom.

examples.target: Wie het laatst lacht, lacht het best.
examples.translation_tr: He who laughs last, laughs best.
examples.note_tr: A relative clause 'Wie...' functions as the subject of the main clause, a common proverb structure.

examples.target: Val niet meteen met de deur in huis; vertel eerst rustig wat er gebeurd is.
examples.translation_tr: Don't blurt it out right away (lit. 'don't fall through the door into the house'); first calmly explain what happened.
examples.note_tr: 'met de deur in huis vallen' = to get straight to the point/blurt something out abruptly.

examples.target: Zij heeft boter op haar hoofd, maar wijst toch met de vinger naar anderen.
examples.translation_tr: She is guilty herself (lit. 'has butter on her head'), yet still points fingers at others.
examples.note_tr: Idiom meaning 'to be guilty of the very thing one accuses others of'; possessive pronoun replaces the article but the noun phrase otherwise stays fixed.
